title: Broncos on pace to break franchise record for fewest offensive yards per play
summary: I hate to be the guy who beats a dead horse, but this stat caught my eye today and its worth mentioning. Through six games, the Denver Broncos are on pace to be the worst offense in franchise history. At 4.40 yards per play, they are just beating out that historic 70s offense — the […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos celebrates a play against the Seattle Seahawks during the third quarter of the game at Empower Field At Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Andrew Wevers/Getty Images) | Getty Images I hate to be the guy who beats a dead horse, but this stat caught my eye today and its worth mentioning. Through six games, the Denver Broncos are on pace to be the worst offense in franchise history. At 4.40 yards per play, they are just beating out that historic 70s offense — the same one that went to a Super Bowl. Also the same one that had eight turnovers in Super Bowl 12 and the defense that carried them there still only gave up 27 points to the Dallas Cowboys in that game. Fewest yards per offensive play in Broncos franchise history 2026 4.40 1977 4.41 1976 4.59 1978 4.64 2001 4.66 pic.twitter.com/pLoAk64Jrv — PFF (@PFF) October 22, 2026 The funny part is… I don’t see any Tim Tebow offenses on that Top 5. That surprised me. While as bad as this is, I think they get this issue figured out. They are winning games still and that buys a little bit of time, but at some point Bo Nix and the offense will need to figure this out. While most would point to Nix as the one who needs to figure it out first, I would point to the woeful run game. They cannot keep putting Nix into 2nd and 9 or 3rd and 8s. The run game has to start putting in the work in these drives. Broncos daily recap Sean Payton discusses where Bo Nix can get better Quarterback Bo Nix has been in a slump to start his third season. Head Coach Sean Payton mentioned several areas of improvement for the third-year signal caller. Broncos vs. Cardinals: 3 Things to Watch in Week 7 The Denver Broncos head on the road to battle the Arizona Cardinals. Here are three storylines I’ll be watching in their Week 7 matchup. How the Denver Broncos can beat the Arizona Cardinals In order to defeat the Arizona Cardinals, the Denver Broncos need to accomplish these three key points. Potent quotables Vance Joseph On the young players who stepped up against Seattle and preparing during a short week “It wasn’t our first time. Those guys played last year. I think it was half of the Dallas game, the Chiefs and maybe Houston last year. So I wasn’t surprised by how they played. We had a good plan for those kids. They played to it. Obviously, our depth on defense is really in the DB room and outside backer room. So we’ve been very fortunate losing ‘Coop’ (OLB Jonathon Cooper) early to have [OLB] Que [Robinson] and [OLB] Jonah [Elliss] step up and losing [CB] Pat [Surtain II] and [CB] Riley [Moss] to have ‘KD’ (CB Kris Abrams-Draine) and [CB Jahdae] Barron step up. So it’s where our depth was, so it was almost luck to have that group intact.” On S Taylor Rapp’s impact “Signing Taylor was purposeful for us. We needed a veteran safety who can play without reps. Obviously that was a short week for all of us. For him to go in a game and play 60-plus snaps and play at a high level and make every call, it’s been impressive to watch. His first week in training camp, we saw it, and I was like, ‘Man, this is cool.’ If we can get him back in some capacity moving forward, it’s going to be a big part of our defense. Again, it was perfect to have Rapp in the circle.” On DL Zach Allen’s growth “I think Zach’s been a good player for a long time. I think Zach is taking pride in being a great run stopper. That’s elevated his game and you watch him one-on-one in the running game, he’s dominant in that part of his game. The pass-rush part has always been there for Zach. He’s twitchy, he’s long, he’s got great hips and feet, but the run defense has gone to a place that made him a dominant player. So I’ve been proud of Zach [and] how he’s led this year. He’s obviously doing more for our front [since] losing ‘JFM’ (Titans DL John Franklin-Myers). He is fully engaged; he’s coaching the guys. But he is playing the run game very well and that’s key for him.” Darren Rizzi On the feeling of hitting a game-winning field goal as a unit “Besides gut-wrenching? (Laughs) I think that’s what you prepare for with that unit. Every unit has their different nuances. That field-goal, extra-point group, when that group’s on the field, you have a chance to score points every single time, the opportunity to score points. I think you view that unit a little differently. I know obviously [K] Wil [Lutz] gets the numbers and the credit, and the stats and all that stuff, but I’m glad you’re asking me because I think it’s as a collective unit, I think a lot of times we take for granted the snap, the hold, the protection. We’ve seen a number of games this year throughout the league where there have been misses or blocks. It really is. We talk about one-eleventh all the time, really just every guy doing their job. It’s really hard to simulate those situations in practice. You’re out here in field goal, and you try to recreate in training camp and all that. I’m proud of that group every time we go out there and execute because I think maybe the common fan might take for granted how hard it is to execute all those different things. A 53-yard field goal is no chip shot. I don’t care where you’re kicking it—altitude, indoors, wherever or conditions. So really proud of Wil, really proud of the whole group because it really is a collective effort.” On training kickers to treat all kicks the same “There’s definitely a mental approach to that field-goal kicking position. It’s trying to make every kick the biggest kick of your life. It is, if there ever was a next-play mentality, it’s probably that position, just from my experience over 30 years coaching special teams. The guys that are the best at it are the guys that can treat every extra point in the first quarter just like every last-second kick. There’s not secret [K] Wil [Lutz] had some misses here in the beginning. Just his resiliency just to be able to bounce back and go out there and make that kick I think says a lot about him and his approach. I think doing that, it’s easier said than done.” Davis Webb On what gives him confidence in the running back room “The way we were able to throw some punches against the Chargers and finish that out with [RB] J.K. Dobbins in the fourth quarter. Last week, they were a good defense. We knew that it was going to be that type of game, and it went all four quarters. We got off to a better start and were able to watch our pass rush kind of get off and force five [sacks], I believe. Obviously we wish we played a complete game, but now the roles were kind of reversed in regard to first half to second half. The run game got off to a good start, and then in the second half we can do better.” On if they are able to change how they play when playing with a lead “Now it’s taking that last step of playing the last two quarters like we have the first two the last couple of weeks. Putting a good game together where we can look up and the score is not as close as it needs to be in the fourth quarter. We can kind of stretch the lead out a little bit. Our defense has been playing excellent, and we are looking forward to hopefully trying to accomplish that this week.” On RB RJ Harvey’s growth “I love RJ Harvey. He’s really hard to tackle. He’s special with the ball in his hands. He’s continued to develop as a runner. Under center and in the gun, I think he’s a lot more comfortable, but that’s kind of like the young quarterbacks in the gun compared to under center. In the pass game, he’s been spectacular. Catching the ball underneath and advancing for many explosive gains. He’s such a good dude. You would think he’s quiet, but he’s not. He talks a lot more when you get to know him, and I’m very thankful he’s here.” Under the radar Broncos QB Bo Nix, on the state of his ankle and his recovery and return from the injury: "Let me see how to explain this: I've told y'all several times I'm all the way back. I feel really good. ……

title: Broncos vs. Cardinals: 3 Things to Watch in Week 7
summary: The Denver Broncos battle the Arizona Cardinals for their Week 7 matchup of the 2026 regular season. Both teams are coming off victories due to great play on defense. However, each have a lot to sort out on offense. Here are three storylines I’ll be monitoring closely on Sunday. The return of edge rusher Jonathon […]
full_text: DENVER , CO - NOVEMBER 6: Jonathon Cooper (0) of the Denver Broncos prepares to put pressure on Geno Smith (7) of the Las Vegas Raiders all night long before the game against the Las Vegas Raiders Empower Field at Mile High Stadium on Thursday, November 6, 2025. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images The Denver Broncos battle the Arizona Cardinals for their Week 7 matchup of the 2026 regular season. Both teams are coming off victories due to great play on defense. However, each have a lot to sort out on offense. Here are three storylines I’ll be monitoring closely on Sunday. The return of edge rusher Jonathon Cooper The Broncos were the top team in the NFL the past two seasons when it came to sacking opposing quarterbacks. However, there has been a slight dip in production so far this season. Defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers leaving in free agency was one of them. Edge rusher Jonathon Cooper being on the Commisioner’s Exempt List for the first six games of the season is another. While Cooper and the Broncos likely won’t get finality on his ongoing legal situation until next year, we do know he is poised to make his regular season debut this weekend against the Cardinals. And the timing couldn’t have been any better. Third-year edge rusher Jonah Elliss, who replaced Cooper as a starter, hobbled off the field in the Broncos’ thrilling overtime victory versus the Seattle Seahawks. Elliss was seen in a boot and crutches at the Utah vs. Colorado collegiate game over the weekend. It’s safe to say he will be missing a few games. With Cooper back in the fold, that should help bolster their pass rush. His sack productivity did decline toward the end of last season, but he still boasted some of the best hurry and pressure rates amongst edge rushers. I think Denver’s run defense will also be better with him in the mix. I’m looking forward to seeing him play. What version of Bo Nix will show up on Sunday? To say that quarterback Bo Nix is experiencing some regression this season may be putting it mildly. A few days ago, Head Coach Sean Payton was asked whether or not he was considering making a switch at the position. Payton stood behind his third-year signal caller and pointed out that there are a bunch of issues on offense that need to be fixed. “No. He’s going to become the byproduct of all the finer things that get improved. The improved play from our offensive line, the more efficient we are relative to balance, running the football. That’s our jobs as coaches here. We talked after the game about we’re excited to get that win, and yet at the same time find that improvement we need in all areas. So, it starts with all of us,” stated Payton. Though it’s clear Nix needs to improve drastically moving forward in order for the Broncos to be a contender. I’m trying to remain optimistic. He has struggled early on in his first two seasons, but has got better in the second half stretch. That gives me some hope moving forward. Perhaps the Cardinals game will provide an opportunity to see the old Bo Nix. The Cardinals had a good defensive performance against the Rams in Week 6, but that unit has not been strong most of the season. They currently rank 22nd in the NFL in pass yards allowed per game. Moreover, are one of the worst in the NFL on stopping opponents on third down. Will Nix finally start showing some promise and help guide Denver to a win? That’s one thing I’ll be monitoring. Who steps up to lead the way in the Broncos’ backfield? As Payton noted, the struggles on offense aren’t all Bo Nix. When you look at Denver’s running game to start their 2026 gridiron campaign compared to where they were at last season through the same stretch—it’s a huge difference. The Broncos touted one of the top rushing attacks in the NFL in the first portion of last season. This year, they are one of the worst . That isn’t an excuse for Nix’s issues, but everyone knows he would operate a tad better with a better ground game. All quarterbacks do. As I authored earlier today, Denver needs to run the ball with authority . That means the offensive line has to do a much better job with their run blocks. Moreover, the running backs need to perform much better too. J.K. Dobbins has really struggled. Last season, he averaged five yards per carry. So far this year, he is posting a 3.3 yard per carry average. Second-year running back RJ Harvey has shown some flashes, but the long runs and explosive plays haven’t been there. Rookie running back Jonah Coleman is eligible to come off short-term injured reserve this week. If healthy, he could provide a spark for Denver’s rushing attack and help them grind out another victory.

title: How the Denver Broncos can beat the Arizona Cardinals
summary: The Denver Broncos are 4-2 coming off a huge Week 6 primetime victory against the Seattle Seahawks. Their Week 7 opponent, the Arizona Cardinals, defeated their NFC West division rival Los Angeles Rams and sport a 2-4 record. In order for the Broncos to keep their momentum going, these are three major keys to the […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Santa Clara, California, USA; Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton (left) and defensive coordinator Vance Joseph (right) during the fourth quarter against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Denver Broncos are 4-2 coming off a huge Week 6 primetime victory against the Seattle Seahawks. Their Week 7 opponent, the Arizona Cardinals, defeated their NFC West division rival Los Angeles Rams and sport a 2-4 record. In order for the Broncos to keep their momentum going, these are three major keys to the game they must achieve to win on Sunday. Denver’s defense has to continue their ferocious play The Broncos have been able to grind out tough victories versus a gauntlet of opponents to start the season thanks to tremendous outings by their defense. One major aspect in their success has been their penchant for turnovers. Currently, Denver ranks as one of the top units in the league taking the ball away with ten through six games. With the offense struggling, Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph and his players have shouldered a lot of burden. It’s quite remarkable how good they’ve been given that. To net their fifth win of the season against the Cardinals, they’ll have to embark on another good performance. I’m confident they will be able to accomplish that. Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett has six interceptions through six games and at least one turnover in four outings. Has been sacked twelve times thus far and two weeks ago was brought down five times by the Detroit Lions defense. With Jonathon Cooper set to play and back in the fold at edge rusher, I think Denver’s defensive front seven is in store for a big performance on the road against Arizona. The Broncos have to run the ball with authority I’m extremely surprised with how well the Cardinals played defensively against the Rams. Defensive Coordinator Nick Rallis dialed up a lot of blitzes and they were able to limit Matthew Stafford’s impact. They held the Rams to just 16 points on the scoreboard and were the major reason they won in Week 6. All year long, with the exception of a few drives, the Broncos have struggled mightily offensively. It’s getting quite tiresome to see them perform badly seemingly each week. Quarterback Bo Nix is playing the worst football of his career, the running game has been hit or miss, and even Denver’s offensive line has regressed to a degree. Arizona’s defense has forced at least one turnover in five contests with eight on the season. They’re advantageous in this regard and Denver will have to play a clean game offensively and not give up the ball. That’s one important factor to watch develop as the game transpires. However, one area of weakness for the Cardinals is their run defense . They have allowed 140 yards or more in three contests and are giving up nearly 4.5 yards per carry. This matchup is one where J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and Jonah Coleman (if he plays) need to perform well. Since taking his playcalling duties back, Head Coach Sean Payton has tried to emphasize the running game, but that’s been met with mixed results. Sunday’s matchup against the Cardinals will be a shot for them to get things going right on that front. The Broncos need some big returns on special teams I haven’t authored too much on Denver’s third phase this season. Unfortunately, the highlight player on special teams this season has been punter Jeremy Crawshaw. The second-year punter has been on the field a bit more than Broncos Country would like. Crawsaw is second in the NFL with 33 punts and is amongst the best for net yards per punt and punts downed inside the 20. Those are good marks, but the number of punts is concerning and directly related to the constant issues and three-and-outs the Broncos have on offense. However, one area that needs some improvement for the Broncos is starting field position. I think it’s fair to say that they need a spark. Whether it’s on punts or kickoffs, Denver hasn’t produced many big play that have helped switch field position. Denver’s currently return yard leader is RJ Harvey. Can this be a game where Marvin Mims Jr. makes an impact as a punt returner? He’s earned two All-Pro nods for that in the past, but hasn’t looked as decisive as this year in that fashion. To be fair, teams have avoided kicking to him often, whether it’s on punts or kickoffs. Either way, Denver needs to get things going and start better with respect to field position.

title: NFL picks and predictions: Broncos vs. Cardinals and the rest of Week 7
summary: Welcome back to the seventh installment of Hart’s Picks for the 2026 NFL regular season. For Week 6—I picked just 7 of 14 games right. The only winners I chose correctly were the Patriots, Bears, Panthers, Steelers, Chiefs, Bills, and 49ers. It was a pretty wild slate of games with some major upsets. Let’s see […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos shakes hands with head coach Mike MacDonald of the Seattle Seahawks after their overtime win in the game at Empower Field At Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Andrew Wevers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to the seventh installment of Hart’s Picks for the 2026 NFL regular season. For Week 6 —I picked just 7 of 14 games right. The only winners I chose correctly were the Patriots, Bears, Panthers, Steelers, Chiefs, Bills, and 49ers. It was a pretty wild slate of games with some major upsets. Let’s see if I can do any better this week. There are only 14 games again this week with the Bills, Jaguars, Chargers, and Commanders on their bye weeks. New England Patriots at Chicago Bears — Thursday Night Football This is an interesting matchup to start Week 7. The Patriots head to Chicago with a three-game winning streak, but a lot of injuries to deal with. Chicago, now 4-2 on the season, is dealing with their fair share of injuries as well. A tough game to predict, but I’ll be going with the Bears at home. I think their defensive pressure package will force Drake Maye into some bad decisions. Winner: Bears Pittsburgh Steelers at New Orleans Saints — Sunday (Morning Game) This Week 7 matchup for the morning game will be played in Saint-Denis, France. The Steelers are 4-2 and the Saints are 2-4. I’ll give the edge to Aaron Rodgers and Pittsburgh in this one. I think their offense can be more consistent going up against one of the worst defenses in the NFL. Winner: Steelers San Francisco 49ers at Atlanta Falcons — Sunday (Early Game) The 49ers remain unbeaten and the Falcons have dropped two straight. For San Francisco to be undefeated with all their injuries is quite impressive. Wide receiver Mike Evans will miss some time after coming up with an Achilles injury in their win over the Commanders on Monday Night Football . Even so, I think the 49ers will find a way to win. Winner: 49ers Cincinnati Bengals at Baltimore Ravens — Sunday (Early Game) This AFC North matchup has some big implications. Every team has two losses this year, but the Bengals are in pursuit of their fourth win. They struggle to defend the run, which might be an issue facing Derrick Henry, but I think Joe Burrow and his high-powered offense can find a way to topple the Ravens on the road. Winner: Bengals Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Carolina Panthers — Sunday (Early Game) The Panthers sit atop the NFC South with a 3-2 record and the Buccaneers are in last place at 1-4. It’ll be the first divisional matchup for Tampa Bay this season. It’s basically a must-win game to keep any hopes at making the postseason alive. However, I think Bryce Young and the Panthers can do enough on offense to earn their fourth win in front of a hometown crowd. Winner: Panthers New York Giants at Houston Texans — Sunday (Early Game) The Texans started off the season in a 0-4 tailspin, but have reeled off two victories in a row. I like their odds of getting a third straight win taking on the Giants at home. If they can achieve that, the battle for the AFC South will continue to heat up if the Jaguars continue to falter. Winner: Texans Indianapolis Colts at Minnesota Vikings — Sunday (Early Game) Chris Ballard is out as GM of the Colts after their Week 6 loss to the Tennessee Titans who were winless going into that matchup. Meanwhile, the Vikings enter Sunday’s matchup coming off a bye sporting a 5-0 record thanks to a tremendous defense. I’ll be taking Minnesota. Winner: Vikings Miami Dolphins at New York Jets — Sunday (Early Game) This AFC East affair is probably the most boring game of Week 7. The Dolphins are one of two teams (including the Chargers) that remain winless. The Jets aren’t a great team either at 2-4, but I think they will be able to perform well enough to keep the Dolphins from earning their first win of the season. Winner: Jets Cleveland Browns at Tennesee Titans — Sunday (Early Game) The Browns, even with a struggling offense, are finding a way to win football games. They are 4-2 and the current leaders of the AFC North. I certainly didn’t see that coming. The Titans, now 1-5, found a way to topple the Colts in Week 6. However, I think Todd Monken and his squad will find another way to gut out a tough victory. Winner: Browns Green Bay Packers at Detroit Lions — Sunday (Afternoon Game) This is a classic NFC North rivalry matchup. The Packers have been impressive winning three in a row and the Lions are coming off an early bye. Detroit has scored a lot of points, but their defense still has some issues. However, I think the extra week of preparation bodes well for them. I’ll take Detroit at home in this one. Winner: Lions Los Angeles Rams at Las Vegas Raiders — Sunday (Afternoon Game) Things just keep getting worse for the Rams. They lost to the Cardinals last weekend and will be without star receiver Davante Adams for a while after he suffered a hamstring rupture against Arizona. After three straight wins to start the season, the Raiders have dropped three in a row. I don’t trust this pick, but I’ll be taking Los Angeles on the road. They have to find a way to pull it together. Winners: Rams Denver Broncos at Arizona Cardinals — Sunday (Afternoon Game) Both these teams are coming off nail-biting Week 6 victories. The Broncos, even with all their issues on offense, are 4-2 facing a tough slate of opponents to begin the season. I’m optimistic Bo Nix and his teammates can get things going in the right direction against a Cardinals defense that is bottom 10 in the NFL. I’ll take Denver on the road. Winner: Broncos Kansas City Chiefs at Seattle Seahawks — Sunday Night Football The Chiefs are coming off a bye and have one of the best offenses and defenses in the NFL. The Seahawks are coming off a Thursday Night Football loss to the Broncos and are struggling mightily on offense without a formidable rushing attack. I expect Kenneth Walker to have a big game going up against his former team in primetime. I’ll be taking Kansas City. Winner: Chiefs Dallas Cowboys at Philadelphia Eagles — Monday Night Football The Week 7 slate of games finishes with an NFC East rivalry. Even though both teams are 2-4, neither are out of it quite yet in the race for the division title. Prayers up for Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts, who will be out the rest of the season to get treatment for blood clots in his lungs. All things considered, I think Dallas finds a way to win this one. Winner: Cowboys

title: Sean Payton discusses where Bo Nix can get better
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country. After six weeks, the Denver Broncos have a 4-2 record. That’s a reasonable outcome based on their tough schedule of opponents. It seems a bit better when you acknowledge the fact they haven’t played a complete game thus far. For their Week 7 gridiron matchup, the Broncos head south to battle […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - JANUARY 04: (L-R) Head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos speaks to Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos before the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at Empower Field At Mile High on January 04, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by C. Morgan Engel/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country. After six weeks, the Denver Broncos have a 4-2 record. That’s a reasonable outcome based on their tough schedule of opponents. It seems a bit better when you acknowledge the fact they haven’t played a complete game thus far. For their Week 7 gridiron matchup, the Broncos head south to battle the Arizona Cardinals who are 2-4. The Cardinals coming off an impressive win over the Los Angeles Rams and showed a lot of grit limiting the Rams’ offensive attack. The Broncos are one of five teams in the AFC with a 4-2 record. The hardest part of their schedule appears to be behind them. However, they have a lot of work to do to be playoff contenders. But everything happens one week at a time. This Sunday, Denver has to execute well in all three phases to avoid an upset as road favorites against the Cardinals. Though one area the Broncos desperately need better productivity is offense. There is plenty of blame to go around with that unit. Denver’s rushing attack pales in comparison to how they started off last season. They are one of the bottom five teams in the NFL in rushing yards per game and haven’t had an explosive run over 20 yards. Their offensive line has taken a step back too—with several starters struggling compared to their performances last season. Under the microscope the most is third-year quarterback Bo Nix. He hasn’t performed well to date. It’s true he has struggled early on in his first two seasons, but this year is a bit different. Whether it’s passing efficiency on first down, struggling to convert on third down, or failing to extend plays with his legs—Nix’s production has dropped across the board. Yesterday after practice, Head Coach Sean Payton expressed confidence in Nix’s ability to get back to prior form, but also acknowledged a few key areas he would like to see him improve. “Just relative to third down, finding throws where you guys look at receivers that are more open than maybe you’ve seen. Play design. Last week was a different defense. It was hard to see the down-the-field throws relative to how they played. This defense is a little different, and yet each week there’s a challenge behind that,” stated Paton. The Broncos currently rank as the third worst offense in the NFL when it comes to converting on third downs. Last season, Nix completed nearly 62-percent of his third down throws. His efficiency in passes resulting in first downs was fairly decent at 40-percent. This season? The drop-off has been significant. His completion percentage is an abysmal 48-percent . Moreover, just 26-percent of his third down throws result in moving the chains. It’s hard to sustain drives and score points with those numbers. It’s a big reason why Denver’s offense has failed to take off to greater heights. The numbers back up what Payton has noticed. Denver’s third down endeavors have been disastrous and are a primary reason the team isn’t achieving much on offense. Nix has been the subject to a lot of criticism in the media. Yet he remains confident and focused he will get things back on track. “I just feel strong where I’m at. I’m good mentally. I had a good practice today. I feel good physically. I think it’s going to be there. It’s just in football, you have to get that one game that just gets you going. I think we’ve been playing some really good teams thus far and haven’t gotten that one, but we’re searching for that one game that sort of just puts us right back where we were.” Perhaps this Sunday’s gridiron matchup will be the one that Nix puts together his best game of the season. The Cardinals have forced a lot of turnovers on defense. Though they are in the bottom half of the league with respect to run and pass defense. With a little extra time to prepare after their win against the Seattle Seahawks, I’m hoping that is the case. If not this weekend—when? As always, thank you for reading. Here is today’s slate of articles for Horse Tracks .

title: Lions vs. Packers preview: 3 key matchups
summary: The Detroit Lions (3-2) will have an opportunity to reestablish themselves in the NFC North in both Week 7 and Week 8 as the Green Bay Packers (4-2) and the Minnesota Vikings (5-0) travel to Ford Field. This is not a situation most Lions fans are very familiar with. In my lifetime, the storyline with […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard reacts to a play against Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Monday, Oct. 20, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (3-2) will have an opportunity to reestablish themselves in the NFC North in both Week 7 and Week 8 as the Green Bay Packers (4-2) and the Minnesota Vikings (5-0) travel to Ford Field. This is not a situation most Lions fans are very familiar with. In my lifetime, the storyline with these types of divisional games was whether the Lions could finally establish themselves as true division contenders. But never to reestablish as one. Just take the 2025 NFC North standings in for a moment. Look at them again. I’ve seen the Lions at the bottom far too often in my 34 years. After getting the taste of what it was like at the top in 2023 and 2024, it felt like last place would never be the case again as long as Dan Campbell was leading the Lions. Unfortunately, it happened. Oh, and look. It could happen again because this division is the best in football. It’s not slowing down. The race is on. Brian Flores and the Vikings defense is not waiting for the Lions young offensive line to gel before it comes to Detroit. Ben Johnson and the Chicago Bears are not waiting for the Lions young defensive coordinator to find his footing while seeking to repeat as division champs. Matt LaFleur and the Packers are not waiting to the Lions secondary to solve its problems before attacking it with deep shot after deep shot. No, the Lions are at the bottom. Feel it. Breathe it in. Remember the decades at the bottom. In a way, it feels like this is truly the first game of the season. This is how it was always meant to be. Don’t get me wrong, the 2023 and 2024 teams are without question the best and most memorable seasons of my Lions fandom. But the story of Dan Campbell’s Detroit Lions was always meant to overcome adversity. To get kicked in the teeth. To get knocked down. But before long, they are going to be the last ones standing. Three key matchups. Three opportunity to reestablish . Ford Field vs. Packers’ offense Green Bay comes into Ford Field ranking 29th in presnap penalties with 22 on the season . The key matchup here is the Lions fans at Ford Field against the Packers’ discipline before the snap. Of course, presnap penalties are drive killer for most any NFL offense. But that is amplified for the Packers who have no running game and are last last in rushing yards per game (59.8), yards per carry (2.9), and rush EPA (-0.299) . Playing behind the sticks making the Packers even more one-dimensional would be extremely valuable for a Lions’ secondary that could use all the help it could get, especially with rookie Keith Abney likely to play often at the safety position. In 2025, the Lions were the beneficiary on only 18 false start penalties, tied for 22nd in the NFL. To go with the 5-3 record on the season, Ford Field was hardly the home field advantage that it had been in the years prior. Sunday is an opportunity to reestablish Ford Field as being one of the most difficult environments for opposing teams to play in. Let me just drop this in here one more time. Kelvin Sheppard vs. poison picked The second key matchup was highlighted well by Jeremy Reisman’s question to defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard asking how do does he decide on your poison in a matchup that presents both deep and over-the-middle weapons? “That is the coach’s job to make sure that we understand the down and distancing, the tendencies and things like that. What have we seen? And obviously each game things change. You prepare. These coaches are good in this league and they self-scout as well.” The Green Bay Packers’ deep passing attack is a bit of a paper tiger with some interesting situational tendencies , but nevertheless, it must be respected out of the sheer frequency they attempt it. Last week against the Arizona Cardinals, Sheppard rolled out a unique solution by bracket covering both Trey McBride and Michael Wilson . It won’t be that simple this week as the Packers have two deep threats in wide receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, as well as tight end Tucker Kraft. With the return of safety Brian Branch, Sheppard has the flexibility to pick his poison by game script, down-and-distance, and personnel groupings to put the defense in the best position for success. . @colton_pouncy on his podcast: since Brian Branch was drafted in 2023, Lions defensive success rate is 30th in the league when he’s not on the field compared to 3rd when he is on the field. — Nick Shlain (@electricsnuff) October 22, 2026 Branch’s return to the field is an opportunity for the Lions secondary to reestablish itself, and it could not have come at a more critical time. Cade Mays vs. Jonathan Gannon Lastly, the third key matchup is Lions’ center Cade Mays vs. Packers’ defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon. Mays is set to make his Detroit Lions debut with his first start of the season. Gannon is in his first season as Green Bay’s defensive coordinator and so far he has made some significant adjustments to his normal defensive philosophy. As discussed in “The Athletic Football Show” clip below, Gannon is dialing up blitzes of 6+ rushing defenders at 2-3 times the rate as he had in either Arizona or Philadelphia. "We've never seen him do this." @robertmays and @fduffynfl explain how Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has dialed up the blitz rate this season. Sponsored by @usbank pic.twitter.com/jQ5crONKGa — The Athletic Football Show (@TA_FootballShow) October 22, 2026 It will be critical for Mays and Jared Goff to be on the same page regarding blitz recognition and communication. If successful, it is very likely the Lions offense reaches 30+ points scored against. Consider this Mays’ introduction by fire to the blitz-heavy NFC North, wherein all three of the Vikings (1st, 66.7%), Bears (5th, 39.6%), and (Packers (10th, 32.1%) are in the top ten in the NFL in blitz rate, according to Sumer Sports . Mays has the opportunity to reestablish the Lions offensive line as one of the most intelligent and powerful units in the NFL since the retirement of Frank Ragnow. These are the matchups. These are the opportunities for the Lions to reestablish as the class of the NFC North once again.

title: 7 Lions coordinator takeaways for Packers week
summary: All three Detroit Lions coordinators spoke with the media on Thursday in preparation for Sunday’s big matchup with the Green Bay Packers. Here were my biggest takeaways from those media sessions. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing What Cade Mays brings It’s become obvious that the Lions plan on starting Cade Mays at center on Sunday, despite […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Offensive Coordinator Drew Petzing of the Detroit Lions during the second half of an NFL football game between the Detroit Lions and the Buffalo Billsat Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York, USA, on Thursday, September 17, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images All three Detroit Lions coordinators spoke with the media on Thursday in preparation for Sunday’s big matchup with the Green Bay Packers. Here were my biggest takeaways from those media sessions. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing What Cade Mays brings It’s become obvious that the Lions plan on starting Cade Mays at center on Sunday, despite the recent success of Juice Scruggs. Petzing provided some brief insight into what he expects from Mays on the field. “He plays at a high level. He’s big, he’s physical, he’s really smart. The communication piece is a huge part of playing that position. So, that’s just kind of a number of things off the top of my head, but excited to see him back out there.” Game-day communication Earlier this week, The Athletic posted a fascinating article about how game-day communication works in the sideline headsets , and Petzing was quoted several times throughout the piece. I followed up with him on Thursday to ask how his preferred method of communication has evolved since entering the league, and he noted how a lot of that was through his early days before becoming an offensive coordinator. I think your headset communication is always tweaking and changing a little bit, but I think a lot of that’s developed when I wasn’t calling it. I was in the NFL for 10 years before I called to play and I was a part of four or five different play callers, different systems, different game day processes. I think throughout that process you figure out what you thought went really well and other things you’re like, ‘Yeah, that would not work for me and maybe it works for other people.’ Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard No snap count for Brian Branch? At the start of the week, coach Dan Campbell said it would be hard to see Brian Branch play 70 snaps in his first week back, but Sheppard said they weren’t heading into the weekend with a specific number cap on his playing time. “We haven’t given a rep count or anything like that. It’s going to be more of a feel thing as the game goes and we’ll pick and choose what’s right and what’s not.” Secondary on the rise While Sheppard was prompted by questions on all three players, the Lions defensive coordinator had high praise for rookie Keith Abney, as well as cornerback Ennis Rakestraw and Roger McCreary. Sheppard on Abney: “A player that didn’t play safety since middle school and you asked him to go do that in the NFL and for him to perform the way he did, the efficiency in which he played with. But it’s still so much meat left on that bone, and he’ll be the first to tell you things he did in that game that he wants back, that he wants to do better. But a lot more positive to build on than negative to learn from when it comes to that player.” On Rakestraw/McCreary: “Those guys are starting to rise and as they rise, they’ll create more opportunities for themselves and it’s up to them as far as what they do with it. But credit both those guys, they went out in that game and played a lot of man with no help in that game. And that’s not easy to do in the NFL when you’re called to do it at the frequency we asked those two to do it in Arizona. And I just want to credit them, man, and just continue to build on those things and understand, let’s continue to grow now.” Picking your poison Earlier in the week, coach Dan Campbell made some interesting comments about how defending the Packers’ passing attack is a “pick your poison” proposition. Fail to cover the entirety of the deep field, and Jordan Love won’t be afraid to take his shots. But if you stay in a deep shell, the Packers can also use guys like Tucker Kraft to beat you over the middle. So I asked Sheppard, how do you decide on your poison? Obviously, Sheppard was protective over this week’s game plan, but he did talk about how they use preparation to guide those decisions. “That is the coach’s job to make sure that we understand the down and distancing, the tendencies and things like that. What have we seen? And obviously each game things change. You prepare. These coaches are good in this league and they self-scout as well.” Sheppard also had high praise for Packers coach Matt LaFleur. “It’s a chess match the whole game, man. LaFleur’s one of the best in the business. He has one of the best offenses in the league historically over the last, what, seven years? And it’s a reason why.” Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp Note: A separate story has been written about Fipp revealing the Lions’ new punt/kick returner after Tom Kennedy’s injury . How to treat kickoffs in end-of-game scenarios A hot topic in the NFL is how to treat kickoffs when there are only seconds left in the game. A couple of weeks ago, we saw the Philadelphia Eagles kick to the Jaguars, only for Ameer Abdullah to take the return into field goal range for a last-second win for Jacksonville. Others believe kicking out of bounds is the safer play, despite the fact that it bleeds no time off the clock and puts the opponents on the 35-yard line. So what does Fipp think? Well, there are too many factors to have one firm stance: “I think kickoff roughly takes five seconds. So, if you’re five seconds or less and you think you can go down there and stop him, then kicking the ball to him is probably a good idea. But, then you also get into the argument of, okay, well there are seven seconds. If you kick a touchback, how many plays can they get in seven seconds? Maybe they can get two plays in there. Is that enough time for them to get a chunk and get down? If they have a timeout, not have a timeout factors into it obviously. So, there’s a lot that goes into it. I think some of it’s got to be who’s your coverage team? Who’s their returner? How much time’s in the game? What’s the score? Do they need a field goal? Who’s their kicker? Are you outside in the wind and weather? Are they kicking into the wind? Are they kicking with the wind? All of it probably factors into it.” The Lions spent a lot of training camp working on end-of-game scenarios, and Fipp says this topic still comes up a lot among the staff. Punting for placement, not power With the new kickoff rules, starting field position is significantly higher than in previous years. 2026 average: 30.9 2025: 30.7 2024: 30.1 2023: 28.8 2022: 28.5 Fipp was asked if better starting field position impacts what they value in punters. While Fipp didn’t want to get into specifics, he did note that punter power isn’t as valuable as it used to be, and that placement and coverage are more valued. “I think it does change as you get closer to midfield. I mean, you guys have talked about it, how far you punt the ball from the 50-yard line doesn’t matter. It matters where you stop them or where you give them the ball at the end of the play.”

title: Detroit Lions promote punt returner to active roster, sign new DB to practice squad
summary: On Thursday, during his weekly press conference, Detroit Lions special teams coordinator Dave Fipp told reporters the team was preparing to use newly signed wide receiver/returner DeAndre Carter (on the practice squad) on punt and kick returns in Week 7 against the Green Bay Packers. A few hours later, the Lions announced that Carter was […]
full_text: Aug 22, 2024; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Chicago Bears wide receiver DeAndre Carter (30) returns a kick against the Kansas City Chiefs during the game at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con On Thursday, during his weekly press conference, Detroit Lions special teams coordinator Dave Fipp told reporters the team was preparing to use newly signed wide receiver/returner DeAndre Carter (on the practice squad) on punt and kick returns in Week 7 against the Green Bay Packers . A few hours later, the Lions announced that Carter was promoted from the practice squad to the active roster. “I think DeAndre Carter’s got a lot of experience. He’ll probably step in and return punts for us and kickoffs for us in the game, along with (Jacob) Saylors. And we’ll just keep going as it’s been,” Fipp said. With Tom Kennedy suffering a season-ending injury against the Arizona Cardinals, the Lions needed to act fast in finding a replacement return man, and while others, like practice squad receivers Lucky Jackson and Dominic Lovett, were in the mix, Carter’s experience was unmatched. The Lions did not need to make a corresponding move, as they had previously opened up three spots on the 53-man roster by placing Kennedy, Devin White, and Ben Bartch on injured reserve , with the other two spots being held for the return of safety Brian Branch and center Cade Mays from their respective injury lists. Additionally, by moving Carter from the practice squad to the active roster, the Lions opened a spot on the practice squad and signed defensive back Myles Bryant. Bryant went undrafted out of the University of Washington in 2020 and joined the Patriots as a nickel cornerback, contributing in nine games as a rookie. He stayed in New England for the next three seasons, playing in another 46 games and starting 17. Bryant moved on to Houston for the 2024 and 2025 seasons, playing in another 22 games and starting three, then joined the Browns in 2026. Bryant was released at cutdowns, made Cleveland’s practice squad, but was recently released and became eligible to join the Lions. One interesting note on Bryant’s addition is that while he’s primarily played nickel cornerback for the last six NFL seasons, the Lions announced him as a safety. Now, there’s some crossover in how the Lions deploy their strong safety and nickel position, but it’ll be an interesting tweak to watch if Bryant gets an opportunity to join the active roster on game days.

title: The Detroit Lions have decided on a punt returner to replace Tom Kennedy
summary: The Detroit Lions aren’t hiding their intentions when it comes to their new punter/kick returner. After Tom Kennedy suffered a season-ending injury in their last game against the Arizona Cardinals, the Lions will replace him on both punt and kick return with newly signed receiver DeAndre Carter. Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp said they aren’t […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - OCTOBER 11: Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver DeAndre Carter (16) runs during the National Football League game between the New York Giants and the Philadelphia Eagles on October 11, 2018 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, NJ. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Detroit Lions aren’t hiding their intentions when it comes to their new punter/kick returner. After Tom Kennedy suffered a season-ending injury in their last game against the Arizona Cardinals, the Lions will replace him on both punt and kick return with newly signed receiver DeAndre Carter. Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp said they aren’t viewing the job as completely open at this point in the week. “I don’t know that it’s like totally open. I think DeAndre Carter’s got a lot of experience. He’ll probably step in and return punts for us and kickoffs for us in the game, along with (Jacob) Saylors. And we’ll just keep going as it’s been,” Fipp said. Carter is currently on the practice squad, so in order to play, he will either sign to the 53-man roster this week or receive a game-day elevation from the practice squad. Fipp noted that there were players, like Lucky Jackson, who have punt return experience, but it pales in comparison to Carter’s résumé. Carter, who entered the league in 2015, has returned 155 career punts for 1,508 yards (9.7 average) and 144 kickoffs for 3,399 yards (23.6 average). Carter has had a tumultuous NFL career. Despite entering the league in 2015, he didn’t see the field until 2018. He was rostered by the Ravens, Raiders, Patriots, and 49ers before he played in his first NFL game—ironically with the Philadelphia Eagles and their special teams coach at the time, Dave Fipp. In his first game as punt returner, Carter took a late punt, returned it 42 yards, setting up the Eagles for what would be the game-tying score . Fipp said he’s always had respect for Carter’s resilience and the way he plays the game. “He bounced around, kept on fighting, trying to make it,” Fipp said. “I think we’re in Week 4 or something like that, I believe. It was when Darren Sproles went down. And then he came in, we’re playing against Tennessee, and he did what he does. He catches the ball, he competes, he gets downfield, he’s quick, very competitive. His story is like the ultimate story of just overcoming all the obstacles, and he plays the game that way. He loves playing football. I’ve always respected his game.”

title: Lions mailbag: How will Detroit defend Packers’ deep-ball attack?
summary: While they may not be as effective as they seem, the Green Bay Packers do love throwing the deep ball, no pun intended. Quarterback Jordan Love has attempted more passing attempts of 20+ air yards than any other quarterback, and this is nothing new. Green Bay has ranked in the top-five of attempted deep shots […]
full_text: NFL Football: Green Bay Packers Jordan Love (10) in action throws the football vs Chicago Bears at Lambeau Field.Green Bay, WI 10/11/2026 CREDIT: Erick W. Rasco (Photo by Erick W. Rasco/Sports Illustrated via Getty Images/Getty Images) (Set Number: X164960) While they may not be as effective as they seem, the Green Bay Packers do love throwing the deep ball, no pun intended. Quarterback Jordan Love has attempted more passing attempts of 20+ air yards than any other quarterback, and this is nothing new. Green Bay has ranked in the top-five of attempted deep shots in every season but one, dating back to at least 2018 (they were eighth in 2025). Unfortunately for the Detroit Lions, they have been terrible at defending deep passes. This season, the Lions rank 32nd in EPA/pass (+1.41), 31st in yards per game (80.6), and 31st in yards per play allowed (18.3) when targeted deep. Lions coach Dan Campbell knows that the Packers’ two deep receivers, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, could be a problem on Sunday when the two teams face off. “It presents some big challenges because these aren’t guys that can just track the ball down. They have got speed now. I mean, they have got speed and they can track the ball and the quarterback gives them a nice pretty ball, man, lays it out there,” Campbell said. “And really about 50 percent of these are either DPI or catches, which is talk about explosive. So, that’s the danger in it.” But as Campbell was quick to point out, the Lions can’t afford to just play their safeties deep, hoping to eliminate deep shots, because that’s when Packers tight end Tucker Kraft takes over. “If you’re going to use it to take the top off on some of this, well now you have got Kraft underneath and you have got to worry about the backs. It does, it creates some issues, man, that you have got to be ready for,” Campbell said. So on this week’s Midweek Mailbag, Erik Schlitt and I discuss the options for defending the Packers’ passing attack. What role should Brian Branch play in defending the pass? Should he try to erase Kraft over the middle of the field? Is he best used this week at nickel, box safety, or deep safety—or a combination of all three? And is this the week to heavily rely on the athletic Keith Abney? Or should Detroit play it more safe with a veteran like Chuck Clark? Other topics on this week’s show include: What is the Lions’ biggest advantage over the Packers? And what is Green Bay’s biggest advantage over Detroit? How much will Josh Jacobs’ return this week matter? Will the Lions utilize more 21 personnel (two running back sets) or max protection against the Packers’ and Vikings’ aggressive defense? Outside of the secondary, where do the Lions need to improve most to compete for a Super Bowl? If the defense continues to improve, should the Lions still trade for a cornerback? Given Detroit’s slow start, why should anyone be optimistic the Lions can turn it around this year? Check out the entire show using the Spotify embed below or searching “Pride of Detroit” on your favorite podcasting platform. You can catch a longer version of the Midweek Mailbag by heading over to our YouTube page or Twitch channel and watching this week’s show. In the longer version, we also gave our reactions to Sam LaPorta’s expressions of frustration over contract negotiations .

title: Discussion: Is Sam LaPorta right to take his contract frustrations public?
summary: This week, Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta went public with his frustrations about his contract situation with the team. In the midst of the final year of his rookie deal, LaPorta and the Lions have cut off extension talks after the two sides have reached a stalemate. And while his initial comments to the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta (87) warms up ahead of the Hall of Fame Game at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium in Canton, Ohio on Thursday, July 31, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co This week, Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta went public with his frustrations about his contract situation with the team . In the midst of the final year of his rookie deal, LaPorta and the Lions have cut off extension talks after the two sides have reached a stalemate. And while his initial comments to the local media weren’t very incendiary, during his podcast appearance on “Pardon My Take” this week, LaPorta didn’t hold back. “It’s disappointing that you go out there every week and you bear the risk of getting hurt. Like last year, whatever it was, Week 9, Week 10, I break my fucking back for this team. And then I’m going out there this year, and I’m ballin’, and maybe they’re just not showing the love,” LaPorta said. He later added that he’s happy to go somewhere else if Detroit doesn’t pay up. “So I’m going to continue to do my thing and ball out, and in three months if I don’t get to wear the Honolulu Blue and play for the Lions anymore, it’s going to be all good. I’ll go get paid somewhere else. So, whatever,” LaPorta said. LaPorta is more than within his rights to feel this way. And I’m sure a lot of people think he’s in the right to be frustrated given everything he has accomplished. Personally, I think the more controversial topic is taking this grievance public. By saying this on a podcast, he is creating drama, distraction, and possibly frustration on both sides of the table. Maybe that’s the goal as a negotiating tactic, but he’s already taking a PR hit, with some fans angry over his attitude. So today’s Question of the Day is: Should Sam LaPorta have taken his frustrations public? My answer: During a break in our Midweek Mailbag podcast, Erik Schlitt and I discussed this topic at length. You can watch that segment below. In short, I’m a little torn. On one hand, I appreciate honesty. Too often, we get boilerplate, safe answers from players who are too afraid to say their peace, because of the potential backlash from the public. We get annoyed when coaches give us coachspeak, yet when anyone dares to say what’s actually on their mind, they’re vilified, too. On the other hand, I don’t think much of anything was gained with these comments, other than LaPorta’s release of frustrations. I don’t think the Lions will take too kindly to these comments, so I reject the notion that this puts pressure on them to get a deal done. I think it’s probably a net negative for LaPorta, too. While he may have experienced some relief for finally saying what he wants, the public backlash is already pretty obvious. Just look at the comment section of our news story on the article , and you’ll find plenty of comments asking to trade him or accusing him of being unloyal, greedy, and tone-deaf. LaPorta is well within his rights to say whatever he wants, whenever he wants. And, again, I admire someone who speaks their truth without being overly disrespectful—and I don’t think he went over the top here. However, I do think more damage than good will come of this. What are your thoughts? Vote in the poll below and share your fuller beliefs in the comment section at the bottom of this page.

title: The Lions’ heavy offense will stretch the Packers’ thin defensive line
summary: You’ve heard this phrase a lot in the NFL over the last decade: Nickel is the new base. In some ways that’s true, but it’s really more like “nickel is the new base, when the opposing offense wants it to be.” Most NFL teams still match their defensive personnel to what opposing offenses throw out […]
full_text: (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images You’ve heard this phrase a lot in the NFL over the last decade: Nickel is the new base. In some ways that’s true, but it’s really more like “nickel is the new base, when the opposing offense wants it to be.” Most NFL teams still match their defensive personnel to what opposing offenses throw out there, and the Green Bay Packers are no different. In general, defenses want to play as many cornerbacks and nickelbacks as the opposing offense has receivers. So when offenses are in 11 personnel (three receivers, one back and one tight end) sets, defenses tend to play Nickel — which allows for a slot defender to “match” a slot receiver on the field. So far in 2026, the Packers have played 291 of their 292 snaps when they’ve faced 11 personnel offenses in Nickel (or Dime) sets — 99.7 percent. When opposing offenses play heavier looks, be it multiple backs, multiple tight ends or even sets with extra offensive linemen or defensive linemen, NFL teams still match that with “base” personnel (a 3-4 in the Packers’ case) an extra body in the box. This year, Green Bay defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon’s defense has played 75.9 percent of their snaps against these personnel packages (12/13/21/22) with a base 3-4 defense. No third receiver? That means no slot defender on the field. That’s the basic math being done league-wide. So is nickel the new base? Really only when the offense is playing 11 personnel. This, obviously, varies a lot team-by-team. For example, last week the Packers faced the Dallas Cowboys, who have played 73 percent of their snaps in 11 personnel in 2026, the third-highest rate in the NFL . Against Green Bay, for whatever reason, they averaged 1.0 running backs per play and 1.1 tight ends per play — essentially living in 11 personnel full-time, even more so than their season-long averages. From my perspective, I feel like the Packers caught a break. Green Bay, which almost always carries five interior defensive linemen on a 48-man gameday roster, was only able to carry four big bodies for the game because of Javon Hargrave and Jonathan Ford going on the injured reserve. Rookie Chris McClellan had to take over the starting 3-4 nose tackle spot in “base” looks for the first time, in place of Ford, and the only defensive lineman on the sideline when the starters were out there for limited 3-4 defense looks was Anthony Campbell, who had played all of nine career NFL snaps coming into the game. On top of that, Green Bay’s Will linebacker position is a rotation between Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper right now, as starter Edgerrin Cooper is now on the injured reserve. Campbell ended up playing 32 defensive snaps for the Packers in Week 6, even with the Cowboys playing mostly 11 personnel looks that mostly kept Green Bay to playing two defensive tackles at a time for most of the game. With how the Packers’ lack of depth at the position played out on the defensive line, Dallas should have tried to wear out Green Bay’s lack of numbers with multiple tight end looks (with slot defender Javon Bullard sidelined because of personnel matching) and tried to win that game in the second half against an exhausted front. Instead, Bullard played six of every seven snaps against the Cowboys. The Packers dodged a bullet, but that doesn’t mean that they’re out of the woods. This week, they’ll play a Detroit Lions team that likes to play a much heavier form of offense than Dallas. The Lions only play 11 personnel 58 percent of the time, a below-average rate in the NFL. They like to use multiple tight ends, or even linemen (both offensive or defensive) instead of that extra slot receiver. They don’t use multiple backs (average 1.0 backs played per play), but they play a second tight end (or extra lineman) close to every other play (1.5 tight ends per play). It will be interesting to see if the Packers call up one of their two practice squad interior defensive linemen, David Blay Jr. or Mazi Smith, to add some depth to the game-day roster this week, but if Green Bay doesn’t, they’ll have to make it through with four linemen for a second straight game. This time, though, they won’t be playing against a team that just wants to play with a full-time slot receiver, they’ll be going against an offense that wants to play heavy offensive looks about every other play, the same looks that have forced an extra defensive lineman on the field for more than three-quarters of the Packers’ defensive snaps in those situations throughout the season.

full_text: (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers made an interesting move on Thursday, as they brought in two punters for tryouts. Generally, the Packers only bring in visitors on Mondays or Tuesdays, which made this Thursday set of tryouts stick out. Punter Daniel Whelan also isn’t injured, according to the Packers’ most recent injury report , which makes this situation even more head-scratching. Maybe Green Bay is just keeping their emergency list updated, but this timing is still a little out of the ordinary. The players the Packers bought in were Jack Stonehouse and James Rendell, both 2026 undrafted free agents. Stonehouse is the cousin of Ryan Stonehouse, who played for the Tennessee Titans for three years and was named an All-Pro as a rookie. Jack signed with Houston in post-draft free agency and was waived by the team in August. Since then, he’s worked out for the Washington Commanders and Minnesota Vikings. Rendell is an international player from Australia, so he would count as an international exemption (in place of Krieg) if signed to the Packers’ practice squad. summary: In the pre-practice press conference, Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur wouldn’t commit one way or another on whether tight end Luke Musgrave, who has spent the entire regular season on the physically unable to perform list with a neck injury, will come back this season. Here was LaFleur’s full quote on whether Musgrave […]
full_text: (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In the pre-practice press conference, Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur wouldn’t commit one way or another on whether tight end Luke Musgrave, who has spent the entire regular season on the physically unable to perform list with a neck injury, will come back this season. Here was LaFleur’s full quote on whether Musgrave will be back in 2026: That’s tough to say right now. Until proven otherwise, I would say no, but I would never close the door on that. Whatever neck injury Musgrave has suffered, it seems to be serious. On the injury report today, the only changes were that quarterback Jordan Love (back) was elevated to a full participant, while both linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin) and edge defender Lukas Van Ness (illness) popped up as limited for the first time. The only non-participant in the Packers’ practice today was receiver Bo Melton, who is also dealing with a back injury. Jordan Love upgraded to a full participant plus a couple of additions to the injury report and only one DNP. pic.twitter.com/GK5c1mOUX2 — Rob Demovsky (@RobDemovsky) October 22, 2026 For the most part, it looks like the 53-man roster (really a 50-man roster right now, with the expectation that running back Josh Jacobs will be added to the active roster at some point this week) should be good to go — with the possible exception of Melton — against the Detroit Lions. If you’re wondering about the offensive line situation, the Packers repped their normal line of Jordan Morgan-Laken Tomlinson-Sean Rhyan-Travis Glover-Anthony Belton (left to right) with the additions of Aaron Banks and Kevin Zeitler with the first-team unit in the media-open portion of practice, according to Tom Silverstein of the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel . Green Bay’s guard combo of Tomlinson and Glover struggled against the Dallas Cowboys ( as we broke down in depth earlier today ), so I wouldn’t be shocked if Banks and/or Zeitler end up getting a look against Detroit.

title: Let’s talk about Wisconsin game day beer
summary: Earlier this week we published a series of game day guides which provide recommendations for activities in and around NFL stadia. I wrote the section for Green Bay, and I hope it’s helpful to anyone traveling to Lambeau for a game, but there is one specific thing I wish I’d spent a bit more time […]
full_text: Tony Rieck (left), of Chandler AZ, but grew up in Grafton, WI, and Ben Barron, of Huntley, IL both wear Packers quarterback Jordan Love jerseys while holding New Glarus Spotted Cow Beer before the Green Bay Packers play the Chicago Bears on Sunday, Sept. 10, 2023 at Soldier Field in Chicago. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Earlier this week we published a series of game day guides which provide recommendations for activities in and around NFL stadia. I wrote the section for Green Bay , and I hope it’s helpful to anyone traveling to Lambeau for a game, but there is one specific thing I wish I’d spent a bit more time on: New Glarus Brewing Company’s Spotted Cow, which is one of the most popular beers in Wisconsin. If you’re traveling to Wisconsin for the first time, you will eventually be confronted with a Spotted Cow , and it’s quite possible you are already familiar with it. Spotted Cow has gained fame via its in-state exclusivity and jaunty name. It’s a huge seller for New Glarus, and in the state of Wisconsin, it is nearly as ubiquitous as big brands like Miller Lite, if not more so. However, as is the case with anything in the history of the world that has any amount of hype, a lot of Spotted Cow discourse now focuses on whether it’s “overrated” or “actually good.” I hate discussions about what is overrated unless it’s about the Vikings, and so I wanted to write just a bit on what Spotted Cow is and isn’t. What is Spotted Cow? This is perhaps the most interesting questions, because even though New Glarus describes Spotted Cow as a Farmhouse Ale, it’s not really like a traditional farmhouse ale. Yes, it looks like one with a bit of cloudiness, but the taste is totally different. I’ve seen some describe it as a cream ale, but I don’t think that’s quite right either, and I think this is a big part of the original mystique of the beer. It’s really not like anything else, but it is quite good! How did Spotted Cow become popular? There is never just one answer to a question like this, but I think New Glarus nailed a few specific things all at the exact right time. First, as previously mentioned, Spotted Cow has a distinct flavor, which separates it from traditional American macrobrews like Bud and Miller. This was an important feature in during the craft beer boom when massive IPAs and Russian Imperials took off, and traditional American beers became uncool. But, while Spotted Cow tastes like, well, something, it’s also only 4.8% alcohol, meaning that unlike the big IPAs, you could consume a bunch without suffering a massive hangover the next day. In IPA meccas like Colorado, New England, and the Pacific Northwest, drinking craft beer for flavor profile was culturally acceptable. Wisconsin is quite a bit different; if Wisconsinites are present at an event (like a football game) where drinking is appropriate, they will always be drinking. Sessionability is a key aspect of any popular Wisconsin beer, and New Glarus understood that. They’re not the only brewery to pull this off, of course. Over in Michigan you could tell a very similar story about Bell’s Oberon and All Day IPA, but the third factor that made Spotted Cow this popular is simply Wisconsin itself. Spotted Cow is ONLY available in Wisconsin and it is a simple fact of demographics that in the United States, no state drinks more per capita . It’s not really even close. And so, the exclusivity to the state served to boost them in the biggest beer drinking market in the country via perceived loyalty to the state. Also, there is a fun jumping cow on the bottle. But is it overrated? Here’s the thing. Your reaction to any beer, or food item, or piece of art will be subjective, however no beer is likely to completely change your world view, and if you expect this one too, you will be disappointed. Spotted Cow is, in my opinion, a great summer beer, an outstanding option for any activity likely to go three plus hours (like a football game), and a perfect complement to most summer food items. But your mileage may vary! All of that said, you should absolutely have one while you’re here because again, it’s definitely beer, but it’s not really like any other style of beer. Should I try anything else from New Glarus? Absolutely! While you may debate whether Spotted Cow is overrated, the New Glarus Brewing Company is certainly not. If you visit their brewery in New Glarus, Wisconsin, you will instantly be hit with winery vibes as it sits on a picturesque hill. It’s immaculately clean, and neat as a pin. I used to live very close to Half Acre Brewing in Chicago (also one of my favorites), and while they make dozens of different beers and beer styles, there is a consistent throughline in the aftertaste of their stuff that is almost resin-y. It’s hard to describe, I’m not a professional beer taster, but it’s almost like they have a house style, and run variations. New Glarus has some of that. Moon Man, their “No Coast Pale Ale,” couldn’t be more different from Spotted Cow, but I can also sort of tell the same people were involved. Speaking of which, you should also have a Moon Man . If there is any single New Glarus beer that that is likely to end the phrase “Spotted Cow is fine, but their best beer is actually…” it’s Moon Man. If Spotted Cow left you wanting something hoppier in the IPA vein (but not overpowering), this is that. Staghorn is an outstanding traditional Octoberfest, and Two Women, like Spotted Cow, is kind of weirdly unique (they call it a Country Lager). I don’t really care for their fruitier beers as I cannot really do sours and their ilk anymore, but some people love them, and New Glarus loves making them. Does Wisconsin make good beer? There are a ton of great craft and old school breweries in the state, but I do think it’s important to always keep in mind the culture in which Wisconsin breweries came to be. Wisconsin is full of the descendants of German and Irish immigrants who were accustomed to lower alcohol beers (Note: Remember, even Guinness is only 4.2% alcohol), and value extended drinking time frames. Some Wisconsin breweries do produce worthwhile IPAs, but most also offer pilsners, lagers, and other lower alcohol staples that don’t necessarily get as much attention in the rest of the country. So, when you’re out at your first Packer game, please do grab yourself a Spotted Cow (if you’re old enough), and even if it’s not your thing, remember that if nothing else, it will leave you with room for a second choice. (And as always, please drink responsibly, and do not drink to excess and then drive a car. We have ride shares now, people!)

full_text: DETROIT, MI - DECEMBER 05: Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) runs in side the 10 yard line during the Detroit Lions versus the Green Bay Packers game on Thursday December 5, 2024 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The road was always going to be tough. The Green Bay Packers entered this season with one of the hardest schedules in the league. Fast forward 6 games and the team has actually positioned themselves fairly well despite some early stumbles. But the margin for error will shrink considerably over the second half of the season. A few weeks ago, our own Justis Mosqueda analyzed the Packers remaining schedule , showing that ESPN’s Football Power Index projected Green Bay to face the league’s second-toughest remaining slate after Week 4. A more recent remaining strength-of-schedule ranking placed the Packers third-hardest entering Week 7. The grade begins to steepen Sunday against the Detroit Lions, who offer Green Bay a valuable test. Although their defense has been exposed a number of times this year, the Lions are a solid, well-coached team with a lot of firepower on offense. A division win on the road would give the Packers a meaningful result in the playoff chase, while a loss would likely further expose what still needs fixing. And the schedule doesn’t get easier from there. With opponents like the Patriots, Vikings, and Bills still on tap, we’ll have plenty of opportunity to see if we think this Packers team can be an NFC contender — however flawed we might know them to be. The upside is that a challenging schedule can help harden the team against those flaws before a potential postseason run. While the offensive line is the obvious Chekhov’s gun this year, the broader picture emerging in the NFC is messy, with lots of room for spicy teams that get hot at the right time. That’s my best case scenario for this year’s Packers, at least right now. We should know more by Sunday night. title: Where on Earth was Brandon Cisse going?
summary: What on earth. Where on earth. How on earth. Why on earth. It may not technically be the worst interception return in the history of football, but Brandon Cisse’s run on Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys must have one of the worst ratios of distance covered to yardage gained. The Green Bay Packers’ rookie […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 18: Brandon Cisse #2 of the Green Bay Packers runs the ball after an interception during the second quarter against the Dallas Cowboys at Lambeau Field on October 18, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images What on earth. Where on earth. How on earth. Why on earth. It may not technically be the worst interception return in the history of football, but Brandon Cisse’s run on Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys must have one of the worst ratios of distance covered to yardage gained. Where ya goin, pal pic.twitter.com/e66rbzsZDY — rcon14 (@rcon14) October 21, 2026 The Green Bay Packers’ rookie cornerback got his first NFL interception last weekend, but it was an absurd run after he made the catch. Cisse initially catches the ball on the numbers at the twenty yard line. On an NFL field the numbers are approximately forty yards away from the opposite sideline. Cisse ends up returning the ball all the way to the twenty three yard line. That’s a 40:3 ratio at best . Even MarShawn Lloyd finds that inefficient. When Cisse first looks up after securing the catch, here is the picture he sees. Cisse return, in parts pic.twitter.com/QIAcKmng5z — rcon14 (@rcon14) October 21, 2026 There are two opposing receivers as immediate tacklers. The intended receiver, CeeDee Lamb, has been blocked and is about to get double-teamed as Zaire Franklin is approaching. Rather than running away from the pursuing receiver across the middle of the field and following a potential lead blocker in a race against the collective Dallas Cowboys’ offensive line and Dak Prescott, Cisse decides to immediately go against the grain and cut behind the pursuing player. This is the worst choice. It’s a split-second choice, but Cisse has a worse angle on the greatest number of Cowboys here. The entire offensive line is more medial to the field than he is, and there are multiple receivers whom have the speed to chase him on that side of the field. On his current side of the field, the only threat is about to be double-teamed, and Cisse has an opportunity to press his physical advantage towards the near sideline where both his current lead blockers and also the defensive line can either clear a path or create enough chaos to make a crease. As we saw on the almost-pick-six from Dallas earlier in the game, offensive lines and quarterbacks are terrible tacklers. You have to challenge them to stop you. look at that crease pic.twitter.com/K4NP4FaTSf — rcon14 (@rcon14) October 21, 2026 Look at it. After dispatching with the pursuing Jake Ferguson, Cisse finds himself in a very advantageous position now. The offensive line committed to the near sideline, and now he has a chance to press the angle towards the far sideline but start picking up yardage. Keisean Nixon will have to be careful not to get a blindside blocking foul and do an airplane block, but between him and Xavier McKinney, Cisse will have blockers who can take care of both wide receivers on that side of the field. Then it’s down to Cisse, Dak Prescott, and the Cowboys protection unit. call you Marshawn Lloyd the way you unnecessarily bounced this pic.twitter.com/bkElsUmaD4 — rcon14 (@rcon14) October 21, 2026 Instead Cisse bounces it and ends up in a situation where he has no blocker for the receiver on the far sideline, and ends up just taking it out of bounds. That’s a lot of effort for three to four yards, and it’s not exactly an elite display of ball carrier vision. Hopefully we see Cisse get many more opportunities this year to work out the kinks.
