title: Why Daronte Jones’ defense hasn’t worked for the Washington Commanders
summary: When Daronte Jones was hired by the Commanders in January, fans were upbeat at the prospect of bringing a Brian Flores-style of defense to Washington. The thought was that Jones would install a similar scheme, one defined by simulated pressures, post-snap movement and relentless stress on the quarterback. Alignment versatility was to be the the […]
full_text: When Daronte Jones was hired by the Commanders in January, fans were upbeat at the prospect of bringing a Brian Flores-style of defense to Washington. The thought was that Jones would install a similar scheme, one defined by simulated pressures, post-snap movement and relentless stress on the quarterback. Alignment versatility was to be the the hallmark of Washington’s new defense. Adam Peters added a slew of free agents on the defensive side of the ball along with the Daronte Jones hire , including: Odafe Oweh (EDGE) K’Lavon Chaisson (EDGE) Leo Chenal (linebacker) Nick Cross (safety) Amik Robertson (corner) Tim Settle (defensive line) Charles Omenihu (defensive line) The general manager doubled-down on his defensive additions in the 2026 NFL draft, adding linebacker Sonny Styles with the No. 7 overall pick and promising EDGE Joshua Josephs in the fifth round. Pinning their hopes for a revitalized secondary on the installation of a different scheme with more pressure up-front, fans were excited about the potential of the Washington Commanders defense in 2026. Six weeks into the season, the reality has been a far cry from the one fans envisioned. While it has held up against the run, Jones’ defense ranks 26th in total defense, 29th in passing and scoring defense, 25th in third-down defense, and dead last in red-zone defense. Meanwhile, the Vikings defense ranks second in total defense, third in passing defense, and first in scoring, third-down, and red zone defense. While no one expected the Commanders’ defense to rise to the same tier as the Vikings this season, the idea that Jones’ squad would be at the bottom of several critical rankings, including scoring defense, didn’t seem fathomable at the start of the season. So where has Daronte Jones gone wrong thus far? The answer, per usual, is complicated, but in this article we will explore some of the reasons why Jones’ defense has not lived up to the standard set by his mentor Brian Flores so far. The defensive line isn’t generating pressure The film and numbers from the first third of the season confirm that Jones is molding his defense in the shape of Brian Flores’ scheme instead of trying to install a completely different version. While not leading the league with a 66.5% blitz rate like the Vikings, Washington is still ranked third in blitz rate, bringing the heat 42.5% of the time. There is also plenty of pre-snap movement and alignment changes occurring under Daronte Jones’ direction. You can tell Daronte Jones (Commanders DC) worked under Brian Flores pic.twitter.com/Hw9RWBDu7Z — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) October 9, 2026 The Vikings are blitzing a lot and it's working… a lot pic.twitter.com/drA1vMyG62 — PFF (@PFF) October 17, 2026 As you can see from the second graphic, the problem is not Jones deviating from the philosophy, but that it hasn’t been nearly as effective at generating pressure. Against the 49ers on Monday night, the defense brought the blitz on 41.2% of quarterback Brock Purdy’s dropbacks but only pressured the quarterback on 17.6% of those plays. These single game rates are a microcosm of the overall problem with the Commanders’ defense right now. It is not just in blitz packages that Washington has struggled to generate pressure. Below you can see pass-rushing stats for the league through Week 6 courtesy of Sam Hoppen . Key pass rush stats: pic.twitter.com/8pamEx3d1U — Sam Hoppen (@SamHoppen) October 21, 2026 At the bottom of the chart you can see the Commanders rank fairly low with a pressure rate of 36.5%, and extremely poor in quick pressures with a rate of 14.5% on the season. Conversely, the Vikings rank at the top in pressures with a 48.6% rate, and extremely well in quick pressures with a 23.5% rate. The other thing to note is the non-blitz pressure rate between the two teams. The Vikings generate pressure 50% of the time in these situations, while the Commanders defense only does so 33.3% of the time. The lack of pressure comes from several issues. The interior personnel are better in run defense than pass rush and the defensive line hasn’t been able to win their one-on-ones. Stunts and blitzes have not been coordinated, allowing opposing offenses an opportunity to exploit voids in the rush and coverage mismatches down the field. In addition, the disguises and simulated pressures aren’t working; many times the rushers are either being easily identified or players are still getting into position when the ball is snapped. Bad ball pic.twitter.com/E02WeCy1L4 — chris long (@JOEL9ONE) October 20, 2026 Trent Williams points out the blitzing safety, Purdy sees it and the body language of the outside corner and throws a now slant to Brandin Cooks for 13 pic.twitter.com/BJT802q2Fg — JP Acosta (@acosta32_jp) October 20, 2026 Quinn says the issues on defense stem from the amount of time it takes to make a play call and get everyone set. You see it in some of the chunk plays from Monday where the defense is still moving around and pointing when the ball's snapped — Martenzie Johnson (@10zJohnson) October 20, 2026 The secondary doesn’t have what Daronte Jones needs to run his scheme Back in May, I wrote an article detailing the three things Daronte Jones would need in order to make his scheme work for the secondary. From that story: It all sounds great, but how would Daronte Jones make it work for the Commanders in 2026? There are three keys for success. The first, communication, has been an Achilles’ heel for the Washington secondary for as long as many of us care to remember. Joe Whitt Jr. and later Dan Quinn, tried to shift to several of these coverage schemes to fix the issues in the secondary, but communication errors resulted in continued coverage busts. The second is tackling. While always important for any defense, the suggested coverages tend to funnel passing attempts to the flats and short parts of the field. Effective tackling can limit additional yards and help get the offense in 3rd-and-long situations and also create more opportunities for the quarterback to make a mistake. Finally, you need versatile, high IQ players to execute the first two. Unfortunately, Daronte Jones has none of the three. Communication has once again been a talking point this season, and the coverage busts continue to happen despite changing the lineup several times. Washington’s defense has a missed tackle rate of 11.6% so far this season and after giving up multiple scores, Jones has simplified his defense. Unfortunately, simplified coverage schemes mean less to decipher for the opposing offense. Another side effect is that Jones has chosen to run more Cover 0 behind some of his blitz schemes. While conceptually easier, Cover 0 is inherently difficult to run, as it leaves defensive backs on an island. The Commanders’ 7.3% Cover 0 rate is one of the highest in the NFL, and Jones’ defense has been burned on several occasions when they have chosen to run it. At times it seems like Jones has let the opposing offense dictate his scheme instead of the other way around. you can talk about the late game botch, but Dan Quinn screwed up the game for the Commanders well before that first half, Quinn went 22% man coverage & 50% 2-high (#5 highest) held Jameis Winston 4.5 YPA, 44% comp & -0.58 EPA/att it worked but in the second half, despite… pic.twitter.com/vTLi6aSRPh — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) October 13, 2026 4 DBs in against a heavy front. Daronte Jones has no clue how to set up this defense to match personnel. https://t.co/em5Lgeccd5 — Josh Harris SZN (@matt_umd) October 20, 2026 While part of the personnel issues in the secondary have come from injuries, the coaching staff (and front office) also failed to recognize several pieces that needed to be upgraded in the offseason. Mike Sainristil’s struggles have been well documented; the cornerback has effectively been benched at this point. Quan Martin continues to play too deep and linebacker Frankie Luvu is still a liability in coverage.…
author: John Portis

title: Commanders at the bye: What Jayden Daniels and Washington’s offense must fix
summary: The Commanders offense isn’t a disaster. It isn’t in a perfect spot, either. We’re hovering somewhere in the either, with a dynamic quarterback in Jayden Daniels and an offensive line still (and maybe forever) reeling from Laremy Tunsil’s loss.   The run game can’t get going the way offensive coordinator David Blough would like and […]
full_text: The Commanders offense isn’t a disaster. It isn’t in a perfect spot, either. We’re hovering somewhere in the either, with a dynamic quarterback in Jayden Daniels and an offensive line still (and maybe forever) reeling from Laremy Tunsil’s loss. The run game can’t get going the way offensive coordinator David Blough would like and the passing game is missing some golden opportunities. Then there’s the issue of situational football and pre-snap penalties, which are killing this unit at the worst possible times. What do we make of the offense through six games, besides not good enough. Losing Terry McLaurin is more than a gut punch. It’s a dagger to the belly and the bleeding must be stopped. We can argue that Adam Peters didn’t spend his cap space the right way – load up on offensive linemen, bro – but that is of no help to the current crew. What can be done with the offense as currently constructed? That’s what we’ll dive into in this examination of the Commanders at the bye. The Numbers Total offense : 325.2 ypg (No. 19 overall) Scoring offense: 22 ppg (No. 21 overall) Rushing offense: 125.2 ypg (No. 10 overall) Passing offense: 200.0 ypg (No. 21 overall) Third-down%: 30.9 (No. 31 overall) Red-zone% : 50.0 (No. 22 overall Biggest weakness Blaming the offensive line is low-hanging fruit. It’s the easiest cop out for skill players not doing their job, and not always the right answer to the question being asked. In this instance, it seems warranted. It’s not, however, the players’ fault. Losing elite left tackle Laremy Tunsil was a haymaker to the dome. It’s hard to recover from that. The center debacle has been rough, as have injuries to top-tier right guard Sam Cosmi. The Commanders are allowing pressure 39.9% of the time . Not great. Their rushing yards before contact are skewed by Jayden Daniels, but the backs aren’t getting much time to work before hitting traffic. Greatest strength The quarterback, obviously. While it’s clear that Jayden Daniels has left a ton on the table , has made major mistakes in terms of situational awareness and isn’t always seeing open receivers down the field, he’s still top-tier when in his bag. Even when he’s dealing, it’s clear there’s more in the tank. While that can be frustrating for fans in the moment, it’s also a real plus when we’re thinking long-term. If Daniels cleans some things up and gets on a heater, he can take this team to great heights even after a rough start to the season. Assuming, of course, his elbow stays in its socket. Problem that must be solved In a word: efficiency. The Commanders offense too often steps on its own foot, whether through pre-snap penalties or execution errors or game mismanagement or ill-timed play calls or, in Chris Paul’s case on two occasions, literally stepping on his quarterback’s foot. All that’s why Blough’s taking so much flak. All that’s why the Commanders should’ve hired a sage offensive analyst to help him through all this. And, lest we forget, Jayden Daniels hasn’t played many complete games in a while. He finished two straight in the last two weeks, which quantifies as a low-key miracle these days (Was that an exaggeration? Yeah. We’re having fun with words. Don’t kill me in the comments.) He finished just four games last year. The law of averages was always going out 2024’s late-game heroics, but how he performs through the mundane needs to be tip-top. So does the interior run blocking. If you can’t get four yards in a cloud of dust, that’s a problem. Russ Grimm and Jeff Bostic won’t come walking through the door tomorrow, but the Commanders must figure out how to do better with what they have. Let us know what you consider the Commanders’ greatest strength, biggest weakness and problem that must be solved in the comments below.
author: Scott Bair

title: Evaluating Commanders OC David Blough through Washington bye week
summary: The Commanders are in a tough spot.  Washington sits a 1-4-1 and now on a bye, thankful to the NFC East gods that they’re still in the divisional race at all. The Commanders should be optimistic, yet still acknowledge that they have a lot of problems on both sides of the ball, in terms of talent, […]
full_text: The Commanders are in a tough spot. Washington sits a 1-4-1 and now on a bye, thankful to the NFC East gods that they’re still in the divisional race at all. The Commanders should be optimistic, yet still acknowledge that they have a lot of problems on both sides of the ball, in terms of talent, injuries and inexperienced coordinators. Offensive coordinator David Blough is only 31 years old and made the rapid ascent from assistant quarterbacks coach to the guy calling plays. That seems extreme, but Blough has a sterling reputation with Jayden Daniels and several big-name coaches across the NFL. Still, this is his first big coaching gig. And, if we’re totally honest, it shows. Here’s head coach Dan Quinn’s evaluation of Blough through six weeks: “I like where we’re at with our taking care of the football. It sounds like , ‘Okay, yeah, no shit.’ But it’s a really big deal. And so, for us, the only way you get in the plus is creating them on defense and taking care of it. I am very much looking forward to finding more things that we can absolutely hang our hat on day in, day out, over and over. And so, the more that Jayden’s back, the more we can get into that flow, I am excited to see that. I like that we have a package that can work at the line of scrimmage of getting in and out of some plays. But overall, I’d love to see more explosive plays from us. When we hit those, we’re hard to deal with.” There have been moments of brilliance, matched by play calls that’ll raise an eyebrow. Why head coach Dan Quinn didn’t hire a veteran play caller to help him as an analyst or assistant is beyond comprehension, but he left Blough on his own. That has created some issues with the execution. We can lump pre-snap penalties into this as well. The Commanders currently rank No. 19 in total offense and No. 21 in scoring despite having Jayden Daniels under center. That’s not where you want it. This isn’t a tape breakdown post, but instead a question to the fan base about initial impressions of the offensive coordinator. How has he done so far? How do you think David Blough has done to this point and what needs to be improved coming out of the bye? Let us know in the article comments below:
author: Scott Bair

title: Commanders QB Jayden Daniels is back, but will it matter in 2026?
summary: In the first half of Washington’s Monday night game against the San Francisco 49ers, Jayden Daniels completed 7-of-10 passes for 88 yards and no touchdowns. As the 49ers put a whupping on the Commanders defense, the halftime score of 20-3 in San Francisco’s favor indicated that the then 1-3-1 Commanders were going to endure yet […]
full_text: In the first half of Washington’s Monday night game against the San Francisco 49ers, Jayden Daniels completed 7-of-10 passes for 88 yards and no touchdowns. As the 49ers put a whupping on the Commanders defense, the halftime score of 20-3 in San Francisco’s favor indicated that the then 1-3-1 Commanders were going to endure yet another disappointment. But, in the second half, Daniels went off. He looked much like he did back in 2024, when he had perhaps the greatest rookie quarterback season of all time . In the final 30 minutes, he completed 22-of-30 passes for 212 yards, two touchdowns, no interceptions, and big plays all over the place. This despite Terry McLaurin’s season-ending torn patellar tendon , which happened with 2 minutes, 16 seconds left in the first quarter. The 49ers transitioned from zone to more man and hybrid coverages as the game moved along, and in the game, Daniels was able to exploit some real coverage busts with big-time throws to McLaurin, tight end Chigoziem Okonkwo and receivers Antonio Williams and Treylon Burks. From a pure quarterback perspective, Daniels did about as well as you could … to a point. We’ll get to the whole “to a point” thing in a minute. Jayden Daniels with big-time throws to Terry McLaurin, Chig Okonkwo, Antonio Williams, and Treylon Burks. Nice play designs and some "interesting" coverage from the 49ers. pic.twitter.com/oBEO0JORHu — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 21, 2026 In Week 5 against the New York Giants, Daniels returned from a two-week break as he recovered from an elbow injury . While his passing numbers were nothing to write home about (17 of 25 for 199 yards, no touchdowns, no interceptions, and a passer rating of 91.9), he ran the ball nine times for 103 yards and two touchdowns. The Giants, under defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson , are highly aggressive with their coverage concepts (they’ve had at least one cornerback in press coverage on 83% of their snaps this season, and two cornerbacks in press coverage 40% of the time), and Daniels was perfectly happy to make them pay for that with his wheels. jayden daniels: i don't like what i see downfield so i'm just gonna run all over your defense the new york giants: okay go right ahead pic.twitter.com/37wlqOwYzh — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 21, 2026 So, between the scrambles against the Giants and the second-half passing against the 49ers, Daniels appears to be pretty much the guy he was in 2024 — a fully functional quarterback who can beat you in any way possible. Of course, the “beat you” part of that equation is hypothetical, because the Commanders lost and tied those two games. We know that the situational awareness thing is a major problem for this organization right now — it really showed up when the clock ran out in overtime in the 27-27 tie with the Giants — and it reared its ugly head more than once against the 49ers. With two minutes left in the game and down six points, the Commanders had the ball at the San Francisco 17-yard line. It was fourth-and-3, so there was no need to go for the gusto here. If you get the first down, it’s all good. The decision by offensive coordinator David Blough to call a series of vertical and upfield routes, and Daniels’ decision to try to hit Burks at the edge of the end zone on a low-percentage throw as opposed to throwing to running back Rachaad White in the left flat, or just running the ball himself… well, that was questionable when the 49ers had Daniels’ downfield targets locked down in man coverage. Two minutes left in the game. Fourth-and-3 from the SF 17. You're down six. Four-man rush with Cover-1 behind it. The LB to RB Rachaad White's side is spying Daniels. Dump it off. Why are you throwing the lowest-percentage pass possible? pic.twitter.com/ipsyyMc73r — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 21, 2026 Then, there was what happened with 21 seconds left. The Commanders had second-and-10 from the San Francisco 28-yard line, Blough called for four verts, with all four targets running nowhere near the sideline. Even if Daniels had completed a pass to anybody, if anybody didn’t get in the end zone, it’s highly questionable as to whether the team could have run up to snap the ball before the clock ran out, and Washington was out of timeouts. Instead, Daniels threw the ball away, which got him an intentional grounding penalty, a 12-yard loss, and a 10-second runoff. welp pic.twitter.com/O5fTvRRHJ8 — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 21, 2026 Washington’s final play came with six seconds left. Now, the Commanders were in obvious Hail Mary territory, but Daniels never got the ball off, because 49ers defensive linemen Romello Height and Keion White split the sack… on a three-man rush. Ouch. welp part 2 pic.twitter.com/a59gzA4GLC — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 21, 2026 Given previous mismanagements, there was also a lot of discussion regarding Daniels’ throwaway on fourth-and-2 from the San Francisco 13-yard line with 13:08 left in the first half. On the play, Daniels was flushed from the pocket, and he had three defenders — the aforementioned Keion White, along with linebackers Fred Warner and Jaden Dugger — with eyes on him to the sideline. Daniels’ targets were covered, so instead of trying to run to the sticks, he threw the ball away. There was a post-snap flag thrown, but Daniels couldn’t have known that the penalty was an illegal shift on the Commanders. take your shot… or not pic.twitter.com/arLE2B4iUZ — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 21, 2026 As Daniels said postgame, “I didn’t know. It could have been offside, it could have been on us.” On Tuesday, head coach Dan Quinn went through all the communications with Daniels. Yeah, I talked to him. I’ll go work backwards. On the penalty, even when you know there’s a penalty, you still take your shot, man, to go throw it, complete it. You don’t know if it’s gonna get picked up. So that was what I expressed to him and as he’s going through seasons and learning, these are all the ones that I don’t wanna wait till the next day to talk to him about. Like, you hit right into the moment where we’re gonna hit. I thought, like most things with him, there’s some plays that you said, ‘That’s an incredible throw.’ And there’s other ones I’d love him to stay through the look to go. I knew in this game that with the team speed, this was gonna be a more scramble-to-throw game against San Francisco. They played more zone, they’d be back deeper to go. So I was hoping to see more of that, but as he’s growing into it, more reps with David, more into the system, I’m expecting his out-of-pocket plays to continue. For him to run keepers off our play action game, that’s a big part of things for us, and I’m looking forward to seeing him continue to develop with that. He always can make some throws that just kinda leave you thinking, ‘Man, there it is. There’s only a few guys that can make that throw or that play,’ and he can do that. But I’m looking forward to working with him as we’re gonna grow through it. And part of this self-scout is looking to see the things and communicate with him too, to say, ‘All right, these are things that we wanna do more of, and these are things potentially to do less of.’ Right now, there does seem to be a disconnect when it comes to head coach, the offensive coordinator, and the quarterback. Blough has never been an OC before, and while he appears to have a pretty decent playbook, there’s the time it takes to learn what’s best for your quarterback and how to sequence plays for your entire offense. Blough certainly knows Daniels from his time as the team’s assistant quarterbacks coach in 2024 and 2025, but it’s different when you’re in charge of the whole thing. So, it could well be that the 2026 season will be more about ironing out all the schisms, and less about Daniels letting it fly as he reclaims his powers after the injuries in 2025 and 2026 that held him back. That he does have those…

(Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 22 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Riggo’s Rag Commanders’ bleak start hides a playoff opening that’s still within reach Even with the second-worst record in the conference, the Commanders are only two games out of first place in their division. And if the team makes the necessary adjustments over their week off , that deficit could shrink quickly. When the Commanders return to the field, they’ll play the Philadelphia Eagles at home without quarterback Jalen Hurts, who is done for the year with a scary blood clot situation. After that, they’ll play the biggest disappointment in the NFL — with the only possible exception of the team they share a stadium with — the Los Angeles Rams. If the Commanders win both of those games, they’re right back in business. And it’ll only get better from there. They’ll face the New York Giants on the road, who they should’ve beaten at home . They’ll host the ever-inconsistent Cincinnati Bengals. They’ll visit the Arizona Cardinals and Tennessee Titans, two teams they should beat regardless of the location. Then they’ll host the Houston Texans and Atlanta Falcons, both currently sub-.500 operations. The Commanders should win at least five of those games. They can probably win all of them if they bring their best. [U]n 2020, Washington started the season 2-7 and rallied to make the playoffs at 7-9. This Commanders team is substantially more talented than that one was. That squad’s regular-season quarterbacks were Dwayne Haskins, Kyle Allen, and a one-legged Alex Smith. Its second-leading receiver was Cam Sims. This team has Jayden Daniels under center. Even without McLaurin, Stefon Diggs, third-round rookie Antonio Williams, and Treylon Burks are still here. And first-year linebacker Sonny Styles is putting together a Defensive Rookie of the Year-caliber campaign just as Chase Young did then . Did a bit of a deep dive on Jayden Daniels stats after his impressive second half in San Fran. Jayden Daniels has played in 31 games (including 3 playoff games) in his career. That doesn’t even come out to 2 full seasons. Jayden Daniels career stats (including playoffs):… — Alex Flum (@AlexFlumTV) October 20, 2026 All the Commanders need to do is stay relatively healthy the rest of the way and let the rest of the NFC East keep imploding. Once they pick up one or two wins, which they’d better be able to do with this stretch coming up, they’ll have momentum and vibes on their side. It looks bleak now. But that can change, and the bye week is the perfect time to refresh and map out the road ahead. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Adj comp pct rate takes into account the number of aimed passes that are on target pic.twitter.com/cB0Mv76opx — PFF (@PFF) October 22, 2026 Sports Illustrated With Terry McLaurin Out, Washington Must Change How It Uses Antonio Williams [T]he reason they need to give him more looks is clear: he creates separation like no one else on the roster, and even though his snap share has stayed steady (hovering in the high 60s of late, even in London when McLaurin was out nursing a hamstring), he’s criminally underused in David Blough’s system. Against San Francisco, Williams ran 35 routes but had only four targets, catching three for 50 yards. All four targets came on third down in the fourth quarter, and his three catches accounted for Washington’s only successful third-down conversions of the night. In an offense looking for answers, why ignore one? Jayden Daniels with big-time throws to Terry McLaurin, Chig Okonkwo, Antonio Williams, and Treylon Burks. Nice play designs and some "interesting" coverage from the 49ers. pic.twitter.com/oBEO0JORHu — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 21, 2026 A glance over Williams’ numbers above makes a major case for him to be involved earlier and more often, including plays where he’s the intended first read. PFF credits him with 69 run-blocking snaps and a 51.5 run-blocking grade, leaving room for improvement if Washington expands his role in two-receiver formations. The bye gives Blough time to make Williams a bigger part of the plan from the opening drive. Give him designed opportunities on first and second down. Washington has a lot of production to replace with McLaurin out, and Williams has already shown he can handle more of that work. title: Betting buzz: Sportsbooks, bettors join the National Tight Ends Day frenzy
summary: On the fourth Sunday of every October since 2018, bettors and books alike celebrate National Tight Ends Day.
full_text:
Everything that happens in sports has additional context when viewed from a sports betting perspective. From season-changing injuries to record-setting moments and so much more, the sports news cycle will constantly and significantly affect the sports betting industry. 

 Our NFL betting buzz file, with contributions from David Purdum, Doug Greenberg and others, aims to provide fans a look at the sports betting stories that are driving the conversation throughout each week of the season.  

 Key links: NFL futures | Awards odds |  Sports betting home  |  DraftKings   

 
 Oct. 23: Sportsbooks, bettors join the National Tight Ends Day frenzy 
 By Doug Greenberg 

 In 2018, the Supreme Court struck down the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act, clearing the way for states to legalize sports betting nationwide. That same year marked the beginning of another momentous occasion that has become a stalwart of NFL betting every season.

 On the fourth Sunday in October -- Oct. 25 in 2026 -- the NFL celebrates National Tight Ends Day, a tongue-in-cheek commemoration of football's most underappreciated skill position. Since San Francisco 49ers tight ends Garrett Celek and George Kittle helped bring the honorary day to life eight years ago, it has become a staple of the betting world, with bookmakers taking extra notice and bettors staking extra cash backing players of the position.

 "National Tight Ends Day has become a fun day for football fans, and we've seen the excitement around it grow each year," DraftKings director of sports operation Johnny Avello told ESPN via email. "This is a prime example of a way to have fun with the content on our platform."

 The sportsbook noted that it sees more engagement on tight end player props on National Tight Ends Day than in any other week of a given season. On the day last season (Oct. 28), Hard Rock Bet says it saw tight ends account for 25% of all player prop selections compared to 11% the Sunday before and 9% the Sunday after. For touchdown scorer markets, that number jumped to 42% against 16% and 10% on the surrounding Sundays.

 BetMGM specifically points out that its five most-bet players for props by tickets on the day in 2025 were all tight ends: Dallas Goedert , Tyler Warren , Tucker Kraft , Travis Kelce and Kittle.

 Kraft celebrated by putting up a monster stat line of seven catches for 143 yards and two touchdowns in the Green Bay Packers ' Week 8 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers . Caesars Sportsbook head of football Joey Feazel said that "bettors certainly prospered" by backing Kraft and that the book has had to be more aware of bettor activity during this particular Sunday.

 "This week certainly will increase the amount of action on tight ends in all facets of the games, which in turn has the ability to shorten touchdown prices when the amount of action is significantly increased," Feazel said via email. "But at the end of the day it will simply be the implied probability of each TE to score a touchdown."

 Even with all the hype surrounding tight ends for the day, there are only four players with anytime touchdown odds shorter than +200, according to DraftKings odds as of Thursday evening: Brock Bowers (+110), Trey McBride (+130), Sam LaPorta (+170) and Kraft (+175). Those could -- and probably will -- change closer to kickoff as bettors pile on their favorite TEs and take advantage of the many promotions sportsbooks will be running for the occasion.

 Sportsbooks, like Caesars, also plan to offer special markets, such as most tight end receiving yards, tight end touchdown combos and other milestone props. Last year, Hard Rock offered leaguewide touchdown ladders and a tight end to score in every Sunday 1 p.m. ET game (+1750), among other specialties.

 

 Oct. 18: Cardinals pulls biggest upset of season, add to Rams' struggles 
 

 By David Purdum 

 The Los Angeles Rams won over the betting public in the offseason and kicked off the regular season as the clear-cut Super Bowl favorites. They haven't lived up to that billing so far, suffering a new low Sunday.

 The Rams lost to the Arizona Cardinals as 13.5-point home favorites in the biggest upset of the season based on point spread. They are only the second double-digit favorite to lose outright in the past two seasons, joining the Green Bay Packers , who lost to the Carolina Panthers in Week 9 last November as 13.5-point favorites.

 

 Arizona's upset shredded survivor pool entries around the nation.

 The Rams were picked by the most contestants in ESPN Survivor contests and in the high-stakes contests Circa Survivor and Circa Grandissimo in Las Vegas. Throw in the  Indianapolis Colts ' loss to the underdog and previously winless Tennessee Titans , and the Circa contests lost greater than 50% of the remaining entries.

 The loss drops the Rams to 2-4 on the season, the same record as the Cardinals. The Rams are the second preseason Super Bowl favorite in the past 20 years to lose four of their first six games, per SportsOddsHistory.com. (The 2015 Seattle Seahawks  started 2-4 and went on to lose in the divisional round of the playoffs.)

 Los Angeles was favored to win the Super Bowl at 5-1 ahead of Week 1. No other team had Super Bowl odds shorter than 10-1. The Rams were +950 to win the Super Bowl on Sunday night at DraftKings, behind four teams.

 More bets were placed and more money was wagered on the Rams to win the Super Bowl than any other team in the offseason at most sportsbooks.

 

 Oct. 11: Who wants to win the NFC East? 
 

 By Doug Greenberg 

 Week 5 was one to forget for the NFC East, to say the least.

 It started Thursday night when the Dallas Cowboys lost outright to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers after closing as 8.5-point favorites, tied with four other games as the biggest upset of the season, according to DraftKings odds.

 Not only were the Cowboys heavily backed on the spread and in moneyline parlays at multiple sportsbooks, they were also the most popular pick in both ESPN Survivor (40% of the remaining field) and the $1,000-per-entry Circa Survivor (2,554 entries, 42.8% of the remaining field). It's the third time in the season's first five weeks that ESPN Survivor's most popular pick lost.

 But the misery didn't end there for the division. The Philadelphia Eagles led off the day in London by seemingly notching a winning field goal with eight seconds left against the Jacksonville Jaguars , giving them a 99.5% chance to win the game, per ESPN Analytics.

 Jacksonville returned the ensuing kickoff to the Philadelphia 35-yard line with one second left, allowing the Jags to kick a winning field goal as time expired. It was the first game in the Super Bowl era that featured two go-ahead field goals in the final 10 seconds of the fourth quarter, according to ESPN Research.

 Then, there was the most bizarre result of the week, possibly the season. The New York Giants and Washington Commanders played a mistake-ridden game into an overtime where neither team scored, including in the matchup's final moments when the Commanders somehow ran out the clock while in field goal range.

 "In the closing minutes and overtime, the live moneyline market was in complete chaos," Joey Feazel, Caesars Sportsbook head of football, told ESPN via email. "Every big play looked like it might decide the game and the book's fate, only for the final whistle to leave everyone staring at the screen wondering what had just happened. It was 90-plus minutes of drama, countless swings in perceived win probability, and in the end, nobody got the outcome they were expecting."

 That's right: None of the NFC East teams recorded a win in Week 5 ... despite two of the teams playing each other.

 Going into "Thursday Night Football," the Cowboys had been the +105 favorites to win the division and immediately dropped to +164 following their upset loss, tying them with the Eagles. After Week 5, Philadelphia is now the slight favorite for the division at…

title: Inside Marvin Harrison Jr.s' exit from the Cardinals
summary: Harrison never reached his potential in Arizona, but all sides are hoping for a fresh start moving forward.
full_text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- The day started like any other Saturday for Marvin Harrison Jr .

 He showed up to the Arizona Cardinals' facility in the morning and went through his routine on the Jugs machine. But that's when his day -- and career in Arizona -- veered off course.

 The players broke off into a series of meetings, first by position, then by offense and defense, and finally, the full team meeting led by coach Mike LaFleur. Harrison wasn't in any of them.

 It was during the team meeting that LaFleur shared the news that Harrison already knew: After two seasons and four games with the Cardinals, the fourth overall pick in 2024 was being traded.

 When the team returned to the locker room, they found Harrison cleaning out his locker. Teammates dapped him up and wished him well. When one player asked Harrison where he was headed, Harrison said he didn't know exactly, just that he thought it might be the Houston Texans . Then he offered up some New Balance gear provided by his sponsor to his teammates, a parting gift of sorts.

 Harrison's tenure with the Cardinals ended the moment he walked out of Arizona's facility that Saturday. He didn't attend the team's Saturday night meetings at their hotel, sources told ESPN.

 He was inactive when the Cardinals hosted the Detroit Lions the following day as speculation swirled around the league about Harrison's destination, with most signs pointing to Houston.

 Moments after the Texans defeated the Tennessee Titans on Oct. 11, Houston coach DeMeco Ryans confirmed the news.

 "You guys want to know? Huh?" Ryans said. "Yes, alright, we traded for Marvin Harrison."

 

 The trade that sent Harrison and a 2027 sixth-round pick to the Texans for picks in the second and seventh rounds next year had been agreed upon on Friday, Oct. 9, Texans general manager Nick Caserio said on 95.7 The Fan in Houston. But, Caserio said, Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort didn't want to tell Harrison where he was headed until after the game against the Lions.

 Ryans' announcement, however, blew the cover off that plan as the Cardinals game was just starting.

 Harrison's career in Arizona ended with promise unfulfilled and more questions than answers. The 6-foot-3, 220-pound son of former Indianapolis Colts Hall of Famer Marvin Sr. was supposed to be the Cards' next great receiver, following Larry Fitzgerald , who was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame this year. But after catching 62 balls for 885 yards and eight touchdowns as a rookie, Harrison's numbers trailed off during the ensuing two seasons while Arizona cycled through two coaches, two starting quarterbacks -- and many losses.

 "I'm a little upset for him because well, I guess it's a double-edged sword," Cardinals wide receiver Michael Wilson said. "One is, I don't want to reveal too much, but maybe it worked out for both parties, I'll just say that.

 "I think Marv was not happy, [and] I'm sure maybe he wanted a fresh start. And, so, I'm happy for him in that aspect, but also sad to lose a great person and player in the building and someone that I have a lot of respect for."

 Harrison played his first game for the Texans on Sunday in London, catching three of four passes targeting him for 34 yards in a 34-31 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars .

 Harrison is now reunited with his Ohio State quarterback, C.J. Stroud . It's an opportunity that Harrison called "surreal."

 "I think it's just a combination of everything," Harrison said when asked why the Texans are a good fit. "I can't pinpoint one thing."

 How Wilson's emergence impacted Harrison 
 Around mid-September, Harrison began reaching out to agents with the goal of hiring one who could facilitate a trade.

 Until then, Harrison had operated with his father as the guiding force behind his off-the-field football and business decisions, but the situation with the Cardinals became untenable and he felt he needed an agent to drive the process.

 

 Through the first four games of 2026, Harrison was targeted just 12 times. He had five catches for 85 yards and a touchdown.

 In each of his first two seasons, Harrison had 27 targets through his first four games, which led to 15 catches for 243 yards and four touchdowns in 2024 and 16 catches for 206 yards and two touchdowns last season.

 Meanwhile, as Harrison struggled to find consistency, Wilson was emerging. He went from 58 targets as a rookie in 2023 to 71 in 2024 and 126 last year, when he had 1,006 receiving yards and seven touchdowns. The Cardinals rewarded him with a three-year, $75 million extension on Sept. 3.

 Meanwhile, things were trending in the wrong direction for Harrison, who was concerned with the quarterback situation. The uncertainty of how long Jacoby Brissett would be starting this season, and whether Brissett was part of Arizona's long-term plans, weighed on Harrison.

 In addition, Harrison wasn't sure how rookie quarterback Carson Beck was going to pan out. The question of whether Arizona would completely pivot at quarterback this offseason and either draft a new signal-caller or sign one also factored into Harrison's decision to hire Todd France and Tory Dandy around four weeks ago. The NFLPA officially added them as Harrison's representation on Sept. 23.

 Once hired, their first order of business was to make contact with Ossenfort to let him know that Harrison now had agents and that Harrison wanted to be traded. The plan was to keep news of Harrison hiring agents a secret to avoid speculation that could create a hindrance to getting a deal done. The goal was to get Harrison out of Arizona as quietly and smoothly as possible.

 

 However, during an initial conversation on Friday, Sept. 25, Ossenfort said the Cardinals didn't have any interest in trading Harrison. By Sept. 28, it was being discussed by the agents and GM that other teams were inquiring about Harrison.

 Harrison's agents did not make a formal trade request but were given permission to shop the receiver, a process which went on for the next two weeks.

 By the time the news that Harrison hired an agent got out on Oct. 8, the Cardinals had already received multiple offers and Ossenfort was far enough down a path to trading Harrison that the news wouldn't deter what was becoming inevitable.

 The morning after the trade with the Texans was in place, Ossenfort let Harrison and his team know he was set to be moved, but the deal wouldn't be official until after Sunday's game against the Lions.

 Both sides look forward after Harrison's exit from Cards 
 When asked after the loss to the Lions why the Cardinals failed to unlock Harrison under his guidance, LaFleur said: "I'm not going to totally get into that right now."

full_text:
The throwbacks were well-represented in Week 6 of the NFL slate. While that's still the case this week, it's the alternates that lead the way -- including two monochromatic looks from the Houston Texans and Detroit Lions .

 

 Houston will be wearing its "battle red" combination, which the team first unveiled in 2024. It's all red from head to toe complete with a similarly colored matte lid that includes a new bullhorn logo. The numbers are deep steel blue with a liberty white trim, while the red pants boast blue and white stripes. The  New York Giants will counter with all-white.

Detroit first wore black uniforms in 1948 before bringing it back in 2005 as an alternate. The team stopped wearing them after the 2007 season before returning it in 2024. 

 The Dallas Cowboys will don their color rush look against the Philadelphia Eagles on "Monday Night Football." Dallas unveiled these threads in 2015 with a silver helmet before an arctic white one debuted in 2022. The all-white combination has navy blue numbers and on the shoulder for a neat look.

 The Seattle Seahawks are wearing their throwbacks from the 1990s, complete with royal blue jerseys and silver pants and helmet. Seattle wore them last week on "Thursday Night Football." title: Proposing NFL trade deadline offers: Moves for Saquon Barkley, Khalil Mack, more
summary: Saquon Barkley joining a contender? Brian Thomas Jr. headed out west? Khalil Mack and Donte Jackson boosting a defense? Let's build 11 win-win trades.
full_text:
NFL trade season is about to heat up -- the deadline is less than three weeks away (Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET). We've already seen receiver  Marvin Harrison Jr . dealt to the Texans , quarterback  J.J. McCarthy moved to the Giants , cornerback Joey Porter Jr . sent to the Cowboys and center Cam Jurgens traded to Baltimore . And in the weeks to come, more trades will follow. Let's project some of them with 11 proposals that make sense for both teams involved.

 While deadline deals across all sports don't always have a dramatic impact on the games that play out afterward, 2025 was a clear case when moves in the NFL mattered. The Seahawks might not beat the Rams in the regular season without  the addition of Rashid Shaheed , who kicked off their comeback victory with a punt return touchdown. That win pushed the Seahawks into position to land the top seed in the NFC, which gave them home-field advantage in the rubber match against the Rams -- and that might have made the difference in the NFC title game . Not a bad return for a pair of Day 3 picks.

 Teams with Super Bowl aspirations will be hoping to follow in Seattle's footsteps as the 2026 deadline approaches. If anything, I was a little concerned that there might not be many teams ready to trade away talent, given that 27 of the league's 32 teams still have at least a 9% chance of making it to the postseason after six weeks of football, per ESPN's Football Power Index .

 Then two things happened this week to shake up the trade market. One was the firing of Colts general manager Chris Ballard , which came after the Colts blew a 13-0 halftime lead to the Titans at home Sunday and lost 26-20 . Ballard endured some unfortunate luck given that his franchise quarterback (Andrew Luck) and one of his best draft picks ( Shaquille Leonard ) retired prematurely because of serious injuries, but the two big swings Ballard took toward the end of his tenure didn't work out, with QB  Anthony Richardson Sr . and cornerback  Sauce Gardner both failing to live up to expectations (so far) during their time with the Colts.

 Firing Ballard doesn't mean the Colts are about to trade off every veteran on their roster, especially given that the rest of the front office staff and head coach Shane Steichen still remain, but there's less of a mandate to try to win this season than there would have been with Ballard at the helm. Indy has several pending free agents who could be appealing to opposing teams, and there might be a scenario in which the 2027 version of this franchise has Mannings in the front office and on the football field.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 And then in Philadelphia, we found out that quarterback  Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season because of deep vein thrombosis. This was already beginning to feel like a lost season for the Eagles, who were missing as many as nine potential starters in Sunday's loss to the Panthers , but the news that Hurts won't be returning anytime soon only reaffirms that Philadelphia needs to start thinking about 2027. Barring a stunning turn from Tanner McKee , who struggled badly against Carolina, the Eagles don't have any sort of meaningful ceiling this season beyond potentially competing to win a moribund NFC East with a seven- or eight-win season.

 This is typically the time of year when GM Howie Roseman calls around on veterans to add to his roster in advance of a playoff push. This season, he's more likely to be the one fielding those calls, and he can't afford to be timid or unrealistic. This Eagles team was flawed even before the Hurts injury. The offensive line, which has long been at the core of so many great Philly teams, has fallen apart. With Lane Johnson retired , Jurgens traded, and questions about the future for  Landon Dickerson and Tyler Steen , the Eagles could need at least two and as many as four new starting linemen next offseason.

 They'll also need to work on contracts for young defensive standouts such as  Quinyon Mitchell , Jalyx Hunt  and Cooper DeJean , which will cause the Eagles to skew far more heavily toward spending on defense after going in the opposite direction. And factoring in the players we already expect not to be back on the roster in 2027, Philly could be at $80 million in dead money on next season's cap. Roseman could push money into the future to avoid problems there, but it wouldn't be a surprise to see the Eagles try to create an advantageous situation in 2028 and beyond by taking a year to reset their cap, as they did in 2021.

 With a need to address multiple spots along the O-line, add depth on defense and potentially line up a long-term replacement for Hurts, Roseman has his work cut out for him over the next 12 months. Adding draft capital would help that process. It wouldn't be a surprise to see the Eagles listen to offers for their pending free agents, and we'll have a trade or two in that direction later in the column. I just wouldn't expect them to move cornerstone players such as Mitchell,  DeVonta Smith , Jordan Mailata  or Jalen Carter .

 I have to start today, though, with a player whose status on the 2027 roster is still up for grabs. Adding him was a masterstroke that elevated the roster and sank the hearts of Philly's division rivals. He was the perfect addition to the team in 2024. But ... is Saquon Barkley going to be on the Eagles in 2027? And if not, would Roseman consider trading his star RB in lieu of losing him for nothing as a cap casualty next offseason?

 Barkley was a deserving Offensive Player of the Year candidate in 2024, but he wasn't anywhere near as effective as a runner behind a much worse offensive line in 2025, averaging 4.1 yards per carry (down from 5.8). He has been in and out of the lineup in 2026 because of injuries and turns 30 in February. He's not likely to carry Philadelphia very far over the rest of the 2026 season, given that the line is missing multiple starters and the Eagles won't have their starting quarterback the rest of the way.

 Barkley is owed $16 million next year, $2.5 million of which is fully guaranteed. That's not an exorbitant sum for a great running back, but I'm not sure the Eagles as constructed in 2027 are going to be in position to get the most out of his talents in the way they were in 2024. Roseman might prefer to use that $16 million to fix what has gone wrong at the line of scrimmage and trust his ability to find a useful back in free agency or in the middle rounds of the draft, as Philly did for many years before the Barkley addition.

 I wouldn't fault the Eagles for holding on to Barkley, but Roseman won't hesitate to be aggressive if the right deal is out there. And while there aren't a ton of teams in the running back market, there's one that would make sense as a potential Barkley trade partner -- which is where I'll begin our annual list of pre-deadline trade proposals.

 

 
 Jump to a deal: 
 MIN-PHI | CAR-PHI | DET-LAC 
 PIT-LV | SF-IND | LAR-IND 
 LV-JAX | CHI-TB | NYG-LAC 
 KC-PHI | NE-WSH 

 
 

 

 Vikings land an impact RB 
 Vikings get: RB  Saquon Barkley 
 Eagles get: 2027 third-round pick (with conditions)

 At 5-0, the Vikings might very well be the team that's actually in position to benefit from adding a star back in his prime. Minnesota has a 90.9% chance of making it to the postseason, per ESPN's FPI, but it'll need the run game and a healthy back once it gets there. Jordan Mason  has already hit injured reserve this season and has battled injuries in each of the past three years.  Aaron Jones Sr . is 32 years old, has already left at least one game because of a knee issue and is on pace for 330 carries.

 

 The Vikings are 22nd in explosive play rate on designed runs, which is a reality of life with Jones in the fold. Adding Barkley would allow the Vikings to use him as their primary back while making Jones a complementary player, which is probably the right role for the veteran at this point of his…

title: Caleb Williams throws 2 TD passes as the Bears beat Drake Maye and the Patriots 30-24
summary: — Round 2 went to Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears.

title: Caleb Williams, Bears find just enough to hold off Pats
summary: The Bears never trailed, but they never seemed comfortable with the lead.
full_text:
CHICAGO -- There were times Thursday night when the Chicago Bears ' lead over the New England Patriots looked in serious jeopardy, but each time quarterback Caleb Williams found a way to rescue his team on a night Bears fans remembered Mike Ditka. 

 The last one was a 21-yard pass to Rome Odunze on third-and-9 from the Bears' 10-yard line with 4:59 left. It extended the drive, and  Cairo Santos  made it pay off with the longest field goal of his career, and tied for the third longest in the history of Soldier Field, from 58 yards out to secure a 30-24 victory.

 Williams put up his second straight 300-yard passing game, finishing 22-of-33 for 308 yards with two touchdowns.

 Luther Burden III caught all four targets and finished with 130 receiving yards and a touchdown.

 The Patriots snapped a three-game win streak.

 

 

 

 Chicago Bears (5-2) 
 What to make of the QB performance:  Williams became the first Bears player with consecutive 300-passing yard games since Mitchell Trubisky had three straight in 2018 from Weeks 4 to 7. He's also the first Bears QB with 300 passing yards and no interceptions in consecutive games since Brian Hoyer went four straight in 2016.

 Stat to know:  Burden has solidified himself as the No. 1 receiver in the Bears' offense. Every catch Burden had in the first half led to points, including his 24-yard touchdown before halftime. The self-proclaimed "problem child" caused issues for the Patriots' defense all game. He's the first player this season with multiple 25-yard receptions in the first quarter alone and put together the third 100-yard receiving game of his career. He does the most with the "runner's ball" that Williams emphasizes. He has 250 yards after the catch, the second most this season by a wide receiver.  Drake London  has 255.

 Trend to watch:  The Bears' defense has multiple sacks (two vs.  Drake Maye ) in all seven games this season. Three other teams have multiple sacks in the first six. It's the third-longest streak for the Bears to start a season in the last 50 seasons.

 Most surprising performance : Chicago stuck with its blitz-heavy approach coming off its highest blitz rate of the season in Atlanta (56.4%), but while it worked against the Falcons, it led to two of the biggest plays of the day for the Patriots. The Bears squandered the 13-point lead they built before halftime when they rushed six on the last play of the second quarter and Maye hit Rhamondre Stevenson  for a 48-yard touchdown. The other longest pass play allowed --  Eli Raridon 's 30-yard touchdown -- came when Chicago rushed six.  -- Courtney Cronin 

 Next game:  at  Seattle Seahawks  (Monday, Nov. 2, ESPN)

 

 

 

 New England Patriots (4-3) 
 Maye had one hiccup on an otherwise impressive night, helping keep the Patriots in a game they never led.

 He finished 24-of-31 for 321 yards with two touchdowns and one interception, while adding four rushes for 26 yards and a touchdown. The rushing touchdown came on a play in which he scrambled, took a big hit and extended the ball toward the goal line as officials initially ruled him short before it was overturned on replay.

 The pick, which was the only turnover of the game and came in the second quarter when the offense was driving, highlights an area the Patriots have yet to clean up this season. They have 14 giveaways and a minus-7 turnover differential.

 Coach Mike Vrabel had expressed his frustration in the days leading up to the game, saying, "We turn the ball over at a historic rate, and it's ridiculous. It's an embarrassment."

 Most surprising performance:  On first-and-10 from the Bears' 48-yard line with three seconds remaining in the second quarter, running back Stevenson was on the receiving end of a lobbed pass from Maye at the 45-yard line before accelerating and then cutting inside en route to the end zone. The Bears were expecting a Hail Mary. It was the longest offensive TD to end a half since Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels ' 52-yard Hail Mary to Noah Brown in 2024 (also against the Bears).

 Stat to know:  Maye's late second-quarter interception, in which he threw an inaccurate pass to TE Eli Raridon up the right seam on first-and-10 from the Bears' 15-yard line, was his third on a pass thrown to the end zone this season. Maye is the only quarterback in the NFL with multiple such interceptions.

 Trend to watch:  Big plays surrendered on defense. On third-and-17 late in the second quarter, the Bears scored on a quick pass to Burden, who raced 24 yards into the end zone. The Patriots also gave up pass plays of 26, 58, 22 and 22 yards, and three 21-yarders.  -- Mike Reiss 

 Next game:  at  Miami Dolphins  (Sunday, Nov. 1, CBS)

title: What's wrong with Bo Nix? Exploring the Broncos QB's struggles, long-term status
summary: The Broncos are winning, but Nix is dealing with the roughest stretch of his career. Why is he struggling -- and is he still Denver's long-term QB?
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- Bo Nix and the Denver Broncos ' offense haven't just taken a step backward this season. They're full-tilt headed in the wrong direction, even as the defense has lifted the team to a 4-2 start. Name the quarterback metric, and Nix is near or at the bottom through the first third of the season.

 As one long-time NFL quarterbacks coach and playcaller put it recently: "It's just hard to watch and hard for them to find something [Nix] or Sean [Payton] can even dial up just to get their balance. ... I don't think anybody saw that coming."

 After discussions with more than a dozen sources around the league, there's a wide range of theories about what's going on with Nix. Some think he could be feeling the aftereffects of two offseason ankle surgeries. Others wonder if defensive coaches are improving at slowing Payton's passing scheme. There are also concerns about Nix's footwork. Or he might simply be feeling the pressure that comes with pursuing a life-altering, nine-digit contract.

 It's all part of the equation as the Broncos approach both short- and long-term questions around their QB. Can they get Nix and the offense on track as they head into Sunday's game at the Arizona Cardinals ( 4:05 p.m. ET, State Farm Stadium, CBS )? And is Nix really the guy -- as Payton has repeatedly stated ever since Nix was selected in the first round of the 2024 draft -- or could Denver be forced to consider a change after the season?

 "I guess sometimes, they can say whatever they want, and unfortunately, I can't say whatever I want back,'' Nix has said of all of the critiques he has received. "That's just the nature of the beast, part of this gig.''

 What has gone wrong? 
 "Bo-lieve" shirts were spotted throughout the Rocky Mountain region last year, as Nix was hailed the comeback king and the next franchise quarterback to follow in the footsteps of Hall of Famers John Elway and Peyton Manning. But that chatter has given way to almost nonstop talk about whether Nix is worth the market rate for starting quarterbacks.

 The Broncos are 28-12 in regular-season games he has started, including 4-2 this year after facing the most rugged season-opening slate in the league. But the numbers tell a different story. In 2026, Nix is 30th among the league's qualifying quarterbacks in completion percentage over expectation (minus-4.0%, per NFL Next Gen Stats), 31st in QBR (38.2) and 32nd in yards per attempt (5.6). Of 37 quarterbacks with at least 50 dropbacks, he ranks 36th in success rate (36.1%), just ahead of Tampa Bay Buccaneers undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels .

 

 Nix is also 32nd in air yards per attempt this season (5.4). That is tied for the second lowest for any quarterback since 2000, per ESPN Research. The frequent completions at or behind the line of scrimmage were flagged during the predraft process by some teams, as Nix's final two seasons at Oregon were filled with such passes. Payton said these throws were not a concern, but Denver is tied for the third-fewest explosive plays (20) and ranks second in three-and-out rate (31.8%) this season.

 Perhaps the most troubling part of Nix's slow start is that he is one of the least-pressured quarterbacks in the league (31.2% of his dropbacks, less than all but four qualified quarterbacks). Still, Nix has had two of the three lowest single-game passing yardage totals of his career over the past two weeks.

 "I've looked at my preparation, I've looked at my process, and I've tried to see anything that can be moved around, be changed so that I can overcome and just figure out ways to put us in the right spot,'' Nix said. "... I've seen what it is like to be very concise, be very crisp on a competitive Sunday, so just working to get back to that."

 Nix has vigorously denied that he isn't healthy and fully recovered from his two offseason ankle surgeries , or that he isn't the same player he was in his first two seasons. When asked earlier this season if his surgeries and recovery, which took almost the entire offseason, had affected his mobility or willingness to run, Nix paused and simply said, "No."

 But Nix has run less this season, and the runs have had much less impact. Nix has 22 carries for 37 rushing yards (1.7 per carry) through six games with no carries of 10 yards or more. Through six games last season, he had 124 rushing yards on 33 carries (3.8 per carry), with five carries of 10 or more yards. And in his 2024 rookie year, he had 180 rushing yards on 37 carries (4.9 per carry) in the first six games, with seven carries of 10 or more yards.

 Nix reaffirmed Wednesday that he is "not scared" and "not physically worried" about his ankle when he runs. But he conceded that "it takes a while for things to fully reengage" and the recovery process from the second surgery -- which he said was six months ago -- is still ongoing.

 "I'm confident in myself, I know I'm going to get back and be exactly what I was, if not better," Nix said. "... My training is going like this [hand moves up] ... I feel as good as I've felt. Actually, I just spoke to our strength coach, and I'm hitting better speeds than I have since being here."

 But so far, the sputtering Broncos offense is 26th in rushing, 27th in passing and 31st in third-down conversions. Ryan Fitzpatrick, an NFL quarterback for 17 seasons and now an analyst on Amazon's Thursday night broadcasts, labelled Nix's work against the Seattle Seahawks last Thursday as "garbage."

 

 Nix has taken a more philosophical approach to the mounting criticism.

 "Playing good, playing bad ... it's a narrative," Nix said. "I think it's honestly something we make up. I don't necessarily think I'm playing any different than I normally play, it's just every once in a while, a ball will bounce this way or something will happen this way ... next thing you know, the stat line is different, and we're talking about something completely different.

 "I'm confident in my preparation. I'm confident in my coaching, confident in our offense, the way we're going to structure the game. I know we're going to have things there."

 Should the blame be spread around? 
 Payton reiterated Monday that he has no intention of benching Nix , that it's "our jobs as coaches" to remind the quarterback of the team's confidence in his abilities. The Broncos are 15-2 in one-score games with Nix behind center since the start of the 2025 season. They've made two playoff trips in his two seasons, and Broncos players believe they would have played in Super Bowl LX in February had Nix not missed the AFC Championship Game after fracturing his right ankle in the divisional round win over the Buffalo Bills .

 For his part, Payton has boiled things down to the simplest conclusion: Denver's offensive struggles aren't just on Nix; everyone has played a part. The coach pointed the finger at himself, especially in the two games since he reassumed playcalling duties from offensive coordinator Davis Webb.

 "I've got to be better relative to the course of the game," Payton said on Wednesday. "... [Nix's] play will be a by-product of all of us doing our jobs better."

 When asked for specifics, Payton added, "Relative to third down, finding throws where you guys look at receivers that are more open than maybe you've seen. Play design."

 A few good weeks could erase at least some of this discussion. Broncos players point to their 4-2 record, and Nix has mentioned the stout early-season schedule. The Broncos' first six games featured three teams ranked among the league's top four in scoring defense -- Kansas City, Jacksonville and San Francisco. By contrast, three of the Broncos' next four opponents -- Arizona, Carolina and Las Vegas -- are ranked 21st or lower.

 "Making it simple, making things 1-2-3, and let's play fast and let's roll," Nix said of his immediate concerns. "I think sometimes I can have a tendency of overanalyzing it and overthinking things, and that's when I'm not at my best. I want to…

title: Kenneth Walker III is thriving with Chiefs. Why did the Seahawks let him go?
summary: While the Seahawks' run game is struggling, the Super Bowl MVP is on a historic pace for the Chiefs this season.
full_text:
Moments after Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III ripped off a 33-yard touchdown run Sunday inside Arrowhead Stadium, the CBS broadcast showed a sign of the rough times in the Seattle Seahawks ' backfield. It was an actual sign, too, held by a fan wearing a royal blue Seahawks jersey amid a sea of Chiefs red.

 The sign read: "COME BACK HOME K9!! PLZ!!!"

 After the 22-6 Chiefs win over the Los Angeles Chargers , Walker sat inside the locker room and scrolled through several text messages on his phone. Many of those messages, from family and friends, included a screenshot of that same Seahawks fan and his sign.

 "That was crazy," Walker said of the fan's sign. "I've never seen something like that before."

 Minutes later, Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes had an even bigger reaction, his eyes and mouth widening when he was shown the image for the first time.

 "That's hilarious," Mahomes said. "He's a game changer."

 

 In five games, Walker has been just that for the Chiefs, demonstrating how much of a dynamic playmaker he can be performing alongside Mahomes. The Chiefs' leading rushing last season was former running back Kareem Hunt , who had 611 rushing yards in 17 games. Walker has already surpassed that mark, producing a league-leading 665 rushing yards, 152 scrimmage yards per game and eight total touchdowns. He joined Hall of Famer Jim Brown in becoming just the NFL second player to record at least 600 rushing yards, at least six rushing scores and have multiple receiving touchdowns through the first five games.

 This week, Walker will return to Seattle, just not in the manner that the Seahawks fan at Arrowhead -- and many like him around the country -- dreamed. Instead, the early-season betting favorite for AP Offensive Player of the Year will lead the 5-0 Chiefs into Lumen Field for a Sunday primetime game against his former team.

 The matchup invites a closer look at why the Seahawks let Walker leave in free agency one month after he was named MVP of their Super Bowl LX victory -- a decision that has been second-guessed amid their 3-3 start -- and how the fifth-year veteran has taken his game to another level in Chiefs coach Andy Reid's offense.

 "He's a stud," Reid said Sunday of Walker.

 Walker's historic start has led to many analysts suggesting he was the best veteran acquisition in the league this offseason after joining the Chiefs on a three-year, $43.05 million deal in March , including $28.7 million fully guaranteed.

 

 Meanwhile, without Walker, the Seahawks rank 18th in rushing yards per game, having struggled to find consistent production with their top two options -- rookie first-round pick Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet -- sidelined with injuries. It's one of several issues that have held their offense back under first-year coordinator Brian Fleury.

 Stopping Walker on Sunday night will be a challenge. And seeing him in a Chiefs uniform, having put together a historic start to the season in Kansas City, might be difficult for the Seahawks and their fans.

 "I'll just say, I love Ken," Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald said Wednesday when asked if he has any second thoughts about Seattle letting Walker leave. "I thoroughly enjoyed him being on our football team. We've had some great one-on-one conversations. I thought we had a great relationship. I respect the heck out of him. ... But I think there's mixed emotions in terms of, you're happy for him, but also, we're trying to figure out ways to stop this guy, too, because he's playing at a really high level."

 

 'We have to move forward now': Why didn't the Seahawks re-sign Walker? 
 As the Seahawks prepare to see Walker, are his former teammates wondering why he's no longer in Seattle?

 "It's crazy when you look at the tape and see, man, this guy is incredible," safety Julian Love said Wednesday when asked. "We knew he was incredible. But that's people above us."

 Walker's game-breaking talent was never a question with the Seahawks, who made him the second running back drafted in 2022 when they chose him 41st. But the team's decision-makers had reservations about his availability dating to his rookie season, according to sources familiar with the team's thinking.

 That helped explain why general manager John Schneider spent another second-round pick on Charbonnet in 2023, and why he didn't attempt to lock up Walker with an extension after 2024, by which point the running back had missed 10 games over his first three seasons. It also helped explain why the Seahawks had Walker split snaps with Charbonnet in 2025, and why -- according to multiple sources familiar with the team's plans -- they were only willing to go as high as roughly $10 million per season to re-sign him in March.

 

 At the time Walker agreed to his deal with Kansas City, its $14.35 million average ranked fourth among running backs (it has since fallen to ninth). The Seahawks did not want to pay that kind of money to a back who they would have preferred to again use in a timeshare.

 Even if the Seahawks were willing to match Kansas City's contract, the Chiefs were offering something Seattle hadn't -- a chance to be featured.

 Over his first three seasons, Walker totaled 3,251 scrimmage yards and 26 touchdowns while averaging roughly 17 touches per game. During the 2025 regular season, that dropped to roughly 15 touches compared to 13 for Charbonnet, who averaged two more snaps per game than Walker -- 31 to 29.

 Walker set career highs with 1,309 scrimmage yards and 4.6 yards per carry in 2025. He scored five touchdowns while regularly ceding opportunities to Charbonnet at the goal line. When Charbonnet tore an ACL in the divisional round, Walker delivered. In three playoff games, he totaled 417 scrimmage yards and four touchdowns, averaging roughly 25 touches and 41 snaps. His 161-yard performance in the Super Bowl LX win over the New England Patriots earned him MVP honors.

 It was the culmination of Walker's first healthy season in the NFL.

 

 Over his first three seasons, he missed games due to a hernia, separate ankle injuries, separate oblique injuries and a calf injury. He also missed chunks of spring and summer 2025 with soreness in a foot and ankle. Then he played in all 20 games, did not miss a single practice during the season and was a full participant in all but five. He appeared on the injury report in only three out of 21 weeks the team released one.

 Was that a sign that, with offseason changes to his diet and sleeping habits, Walker was now durable enough to carry a full load? The Seahawks could have bought a year to help determine the answer via the franchise tag, but the $14.3 million cost was clearly prohibitive in their eyes.

 Instead, they added veteran Emanuel Wilson on a one-year, $1.6 million deal and spent the 32nd pick on Price with a plan to use those two as well as George Holani until Charbonnet returned. Charbonnet could return as early as Sunday , while Price (chest) has to spend at least one more game on injured reserve .

 Before landing on IR, Price averaged 4.3 yards on 28 carries with zero touchdowns over the first three games. Wilson (3.5 yards per carry) has been effective in spurts, but neither he nor Holani (3.1 YPC) have much explosiveness, something Seattle's backfield has missed with Walker gone. Then again, the Seahawks have been contacted in the backfield on 22% of their rushing attempts this season -- the fifth-highest rate in the NFL, per ESPN Research -- which is indicative of blocking struggles that most running backs would find difficult to overcome.

 

 A final judgement on the Seahawks' decision to let Walker leave should not be rendered until Price and Charbonnet have a chance to show whether they can lead an effective run game. Time will also tell whether Walker can hold up physically in a featured role.
